Campaign Length 
                  
                

We are playing seven missions, one per month, and after the last mission, the player with the highest final score wins.
This campaign will run from June 2026 to December 2026.




                  
                  Final Score Calulation 
                  
                

To accommodate late joiners, each warband’s total VP is divided by the number of missions they played to get their final score.




                  
                  Scheduling Matches 
                  
                

Campaign games will be played at Brendon & Mira’s place on Wednesday’s between 6:00pm & 10:00pm.
Each month you will be assigned a match & you will be responsible for organising your game with your opponent.

Campaign Rules


                  
                  Building A Warband 
                  
                

New warbands must follow the Force Organization rules:

Heroes: Only one hero per 125pts. (Continues to apply)
Copies of Same Unit: Only 1+X copies of the same unit, where X is 1 per 125pts.
Most Expensive Unit: No single unit can be worth over 35% of total points.
Total Units: Only 1 unit per 25pts.
Total Models: Only 1 model per 15pts.

New warbands receive 150pts and late joiners receive an additional 25pts for each mission they missed.
Players may save up to 30pts to be spent later.
Force organizaton rules are not applied when recruiting units & upgrading warbands.




                  
                  Mission Setup 
                  
                

The Warbands: There are no point limits in campaign games, however no warband may bring over 50pts more than the value of the warband with the lowest point value. Note that players don’t have to bring all units from their warband when playing a game.
Underdog Bonus: Any warband that has a point value lower than at least one other warband in the game gets an underdog bonus. They get 1 underdog point for every 10pts difference between their warband and the one with the highest value. Each underdog point can be spent to modify all dice in a friendly or enemy roll by +1 or -1, but only one point can be spent per role.
Special Objectives: In addition to the mission objectives, players may earn a bonus 10 pts by completing special objectives. Players roll for a random bonus objective (See AOFS Special Objectives).




                  
                  Playing Missions 
                  
                

Game Boards:** Campaign games will be played on a premade game board, every mission will have a unique board & all matches for that mission will use the same board.
Mission Length: Missions are played with standard rules over 4 rounds.
Resolving Draws: If after 4 rounds there is no winner, the game continues onto the next round until there is one winner.
Conceding: At the beginning of any round players may concede, taking the loss & removing all of their units from the table, which don’t count as casualties for this game.
Mission Rewards: In addition to mission objectives, the winning warband gets 2 VP and 20pts, whilst all losing warbands get 40pts instead.




                  
                  Checking Casualties 
                  
                

This campaign is has a chance of Permadeath.
At the end of a game, all units that were knocked out or routed must pass a casualty check to see if they are permanently removed from the warband (See AOFS Check For Casualties).




                  
                  Earning Experience 
                  
                

After checking casualties, units earn XP in battle for each of the following things:

+1 XP: Surviving the battle. (Not a knocked out/routed)
+1 XP: Knocked out an enemy unit.
+2XP: Knocked out an enemy hero unit.

When a unit earns 5XP, they get stronger (See AOFS Earn Experience).




                  
                  Recruiting Units & Upgrading Warbands 
                  
                

After earning experience, players may recruit new units & upgrade their warband.
When recruiting a new unit, players can spend 10pts to have it start with 5 XP.
When buying upgrades worth less than 0pts, you gain those points instead of spending them.
Players may sell any of their upgrades for half their original price (rounding down to the nearest multiple of 5).
Players may only try to sell one item worth 5pts after each mission, roll one die, on a 1-3 the item can’t be sold, on a 4+ it can be sold for 5pts.
When selling upgrades worth less than 0pts, you must spend their full points cost instead of gaining them.
Players may only recruit one hero per 125pts in their warband.

Games/AOFS/AOFS-Reference/AOFS-Check-For.content:
Note 
                  
                

Casualties: At the end of the game, all units that were Knocked Out or Routed count as casualties.


Regular Units: For every unit that is a casualty, roll one die to see what happens:





















ResultRegular Units1Dead - Remove the unit from your warband sheet (losing all its points).2-5Recovered - Unit recovers and may be used without penalties.6Natural Talent - Unit recovers and earns +1 XP.
Hero Units: For every hero that is a casualty, roll one die to see what happens:





















ResultHero Units1Injury Trait - Hero recovers, becomes 5 pts cheaper and get an Injury trait.2-5Recovered - Hero recovers and may be used without penalties.6Talent Trait - Hero recovers, becomes 5 pts more expensive and gets a Talent trait.

































ResultInjury Trait1Dead - Remove the hero from your warband sheet. (losing all its points).2Chest Wound - Gets -1 to rolls when blocking hits.3Blinded Eye - Gets -1 to rolls when shooting.4Arm Injury - Gets -1 to rolls when in melee.5Traumatized - Gets -1 to rolls when taking morale tests.6Smashed Leg - Moves -1” on advance and -2” on rush and charge actions.

































ResultTalent Trait1Natural Talent - Gets +1 XP.2Motivated - Always passes the first morale test of the match.3Crazed - Gets +1 attack in melee when charging.4Bitter Rivalry - Gets +1 to hit against enemy heroes.5Horrible Scars - Enemy units get -1 to hit when in melee against this hero.6Toughened - Gets Tough(+1).


                  
                  Note 
                  
                

Each talent trait (Except for Natural Talent) can only be gained once, so if you roll a trait you already have, keep re-rolling until you get a new trait you don’t have yet.


Optional Rules


                  
                  Optional Rule (Refer to Campaign) 
                  
                

No Permadeath: In a campaign with this rule, you can play without units being removed from the warband when they die, but instead they lose all XP earned during the match and must sit out the next D3 matches.

Games/AOFS/AOFS-Scenarios/AOFS-Scenario-.title: Scenario - Hold The Line
Games/AOFS/AOFS-Scenarios/AOFS-Scenario-.content:
Objectives 
                  
                

Before deployment, players have to set up a total of 4 objective markers, as shown in the mission diagram.
At the end of each round, if a unit is within 3” of a marker whilst enemies aren’t, then the objective is seized.
Markers stay under the player’s control even after leaving, but if units from both sides are contesting a marker then it becomes neutral again.




                  
                  Deployment 
                  
                

The players roll-off, and the winner picks zone A or B to be their deployment zone, with their opponent taking the opposite. Then the players alternate in placing one unit each within their deployment zone, starting with the player that won the deployment roll-off.




                  
                  First Turn 
                  
                

The player that has won the deployment roll-off gets the first turn.




                  
                  Scoring 
                  
                

At the end of each round players get 1 VP for each objective marker they control inside their own deployment zone, plus 2 VPs for each objective marker they control inside the enemy deployment zone.
The game ends after 4 rounds, and the player that scored most VPs wins.




                  
                  Side Missions 
                  
                

At the end of the game players get 1 VP for each side-mission they completed:

Have one or more friendly units fully within 6” of the table centre.
Destroy five or more enemy models.
Destroy one enemy Hero and at least 25% of models in the enemy army.





                  
                  Special Objectives 
                  
                

In addition to winning/losing players may earn a bonus 10 pts by completing special objectives.
Players roll for a random bonus objective at the start of the game (See AOFS Special Objectives).

Games/AOFS/AOFS.title: AOFS (Age Of Fantasy Skirmish)
Games/AOFS/AOFS.content:
Age of Fantasy Skirmish is a free, quick-play tabletop miniature wargame by One Page Rules. Players build small warbands and clash in fast-paced battles set in a world of magic, ancient ruins, and warring factions. The rules are deliberately streamlined — the full core rules fit on a single page — making it easy to pick up and play without sacrificing tactical depth.


                  
                  Our Games 
                  
                

This section tracks the campaigns from our group’s Age of Fantasy Skirmish games. Log your battles and keep track of the story as it unfolds!



About the Game
Publisher: One Page Rules (OPR) — rules are free to download
Scale: Skirmish — typically 5–15 miniatures per side
Points: Standard games run at 150–250pts
Table Size: Recommended 4×4 (we play on 3×3)
Core Mechanic: Roll a d6 against your unit’s Quality score to hit, Defence score to survive
Each unit has just two core stats — Quality and Defence — plus weapon profiles and optional special abilities. This keeps the game fast without removing meaningful decisions.

Link campaign logs here as they’re created. Use the AOFS Campaign Template to start a new one.

Core Rules
These are based on the Core Rules v3.5.1
Movement
Units must stay within 1” of at least one other member (3” when on different elevations due to falling), and within 6” of all other members. Units can only be within 1” of another unit when charging, and may only charge if at least one model is in charging distance.






























ActionMoveNotesCharge12”Moves into meleeRush12”Can’t shootAdvance6”Can shoot after moveHold0”Can shoot
Shooting
Models in range and line of sight may fire all ranged weapons and may fire at up to two different targets with different weapon types. Shooting models take one quality test per attack, and each success is a hit. For each hit defencing units roll one die trying to score their Defence value or higher to block, and each fail causes one wound. Then check the wound check table to see what happens.
Melee (Charging)
Charging models must move into base contact with targets, or as close as possible, and then the defenders do the same, moving up to 3”. Models must strike enemies within 2” horizontally and 4” vertically with all Melee weapons. For each hit defencing units roll one die trying to score their Defence value or higher to block, and each fail causes one wound. Then check the wound check table to see what happens. Defenders may choose to strike back but don’t have to. If one unit is destroyed, the other may move up to 3”, else chargers move ack and separate by 1” if possible.
Fatigue
After charging, striking back or when Shaken, units hit on unmodified rolls of 6 in melee until the end of that round.
Wound Checks
Whenever the last model in a unit takes one or more wounds, place a wound maker next to it for each. Then the defender rolls one die, adding the number of wounds to the result.

















RollEffect1-5Shaken - The model is counted as fatigued, always fails morale tests and can’t contest/seize objectives. The unit must spend one full activation idle to remove the condition.6+Knocked Out - The model is removed from play.
Whenever a unit with multiple models takes a wound, each wound kills one model until one remains. Only the last model accumulates wounds and rolls a wound check.
Note: For a simple way to calculate the result required to knock out a model that also works with tough, treat the wounds the model is allowed before making a wound check as hit points, then the model is then knocked out on a 5+X where X is their hit points.
Moral Checks
At the end of each round, after objectives are resolved, if an army is down to half or less of its starting units, then all of its units must take a morale test. To take a morale test, take a quality test, and if failed the unit is Shaken, and if the unit was already Shaken, then it routes instead (remove from play as destroyed).
Push Checks
When attacking a model that is shaken, the attacker may try to push it instead. The attacker rolls one die and on a 4+, the attacker may move the model by up to 2” in any direction.
Jump Checks
Models may cross 1” gaps or drop up to 3” without any check but can jump or drop up to 6” with a successful Jump check. Roll X+1 dice, trying to score 3+ on each, where X is one die for every full 3” the model wants to move. If all are successes, then the model may cross the distance without counting towards its move. If any roll is failed, then the model falls from their starting position instead. All models in a unit require their own jump check.
Note 1: A drop of up to 3” as part of your movement does not trigger fall damage as its considered a controlled movement.
*Note 2: After a failed jump, the model is allowed one turn to regain unit coherency before being removed. When a difference in elevation is present, the unit coherency rule extends from 1” between models to 3”. If unit coherency is still not achieved then the offending models are removed.
Falling & Fall Damage
If a model falls or is pushed off 2” tall, it takes 1 hit with AP(X) where X is AP(1) for every full 3” it fell. Then place the model within 2” of the bottom and its activation ends immediately. For units with multiple models, falling kills the model instead until only the last model remains which falls normally.
Climbing/Moving Up
You can climb any surface that is not completely vertical (shear); there must be a path, ladder, staircase or gentle slope.
Cover Terrain
Units with most models fully inside cover or behind line of sight blockers get +1 to defence rolls against shooting.
Difficult Terrain
Units moving through difficult terrain at any point cant move more than 6” at a time that turn.
Dangerous Terrain
Models moving across dangerous terrain, or that activate in it, must roll one die (or as many as their tough value), and for each roll of a 1 the unit takes a wound.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: D&D Campaign 1 - Sunday Adventurers League
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
D&D Campaign 1 - Sunday Adventurers League
Campaign Parameters

Campaign number: 1
Party size: 5 players total (rotating DM — 1 player always runs as Dungeon Master, 3–4 remaining players are active Player Characters each session)
Character level: 3 (update as the campaign progresses)
Difficulty: Medium — encounters are designed to drain resources (spell slots, consumables, limited-use abilities) rather than maximise lethality. Death is on the table for poor decisions but must always be clearly telegraphed in advance. Surprise instakills and unavoidable TPKs are off the table.
Setting: Forgotten Realms. The guild headquarters sits in the outskirts of Waterdeep, on the Sword Coast. The campaign is anchored to the guild headquarters (see World & Lore).

Theme & Tone
Lighthearted episodic adventure. Tone sits close to a heist comedy or tavern-brawl romp — competent heroes who don’t take themselves too seriously, banter between party members, colourful NPCs, and problems that can usually be solved with creativity as readily as swords. Dark moments are fine as contrast but should resolve toward hope or humour. Pacing target: 50% combat / 30% roleplay / 20% exploration. Each session should feel complete on its own — a self-contained job with a clear beginning, middle, and end.
Always Include

Guild contract framing: Every session opens with the party receiving a contract from the guild. The hook must include the client or guild officer issuing the job, the stated objective, and the contracted reward. Rewards are agreed upfront and paid on completion.
Resource pressure: Design encounters to tax spell slots, consumables, and limited-use abilities. Multiple smaller challenges per session are preferable to one large spike. The goal is a party that feels spent by the end of a session, not a party that nearly died in round one.
Clear danger signals before any encounter with meaningful death risk: fleeing enemies, environmental scale, NPC warnings, an explicit “you could walk away” beat. Players must always have a meaningful choice to engage or avoid.
At least one social encounter that can be fully resolved without combat — negotiation, deception, persuasion, or performance are all valid.
A moment of levity — a funny NPC, an absurd complication, or a situation the party can play for laughs. Do not make every beat tense.
A discoverable secret or bonus objective that rewards thorough players — hidden loot, a side story thread, or information that adds colour to the world.
Encounter variety: at least one non-combat challenge (trap, puzzle, environmental obstacle, skill challenge) per session.

Never Include

Encounters or traps that kill a PC with no warning and no opportunity to react (no save-or-die on first contact, no one-shot from full HP without prior telegraphing)
Intentional betrayal in either direction — the guild does not betray the players, and no story should put the players in a position where betraying the guild is the intended outcome. Guild complications must come from clients or external parties, never from the guild itself.
Horror involving children or harm to minors
Sexual content
Graphic torture as entertainment

Prefer to Avoid

Fetch quests with no narrative payoff or NPC personality attached
Puzzles that require out-of-game knowledge (pop culture, real-world trivia)
Extended dungeon crawls with no roleplay beats — break up combat rooms with discovery moments
Strong mechanical penalties (permanent stat loss, long-term mechanical disadvantages) — roleplay-based consequences and setbacks are welcome, but avoid punishments that significantly impair a character’s mechanical effectiveness for extended periods

Rewards

Primary: Gold and consumables (potions, ammunition, spell components, etc.)
Magic items: Distributed via occasional in-guild auctions. Magic items are not standard contract rewards — do not include them as session loot. Auction supply is handled separately.
Contracts always state the gold reward upfront. Bonus rewards for exceeding objectives are appropriate.

Death & Resurrection
Death Insurance
The guild’s Wizard Shop offers a retainer-based death insurance service. Characters pay an ongoing retainer to maintain coverage; if payments lapse, coverage is void. Players may take out this insurance without knowing whether they will ever need it. Details of the service (cost, terms, limits) are to be established in early sessions.
Resurrection
Resurrection services are available but carry meaningful cost:

Resurrection comes with roleplay-based penalties (trauma, visions, changed outlook, obligations) and/or a small chance of outright failure — keeping death something the party genuinely wants to avoid.
The specific mechanics and failure chance are to be set by the DM running the relevant session.

Curse & Disease Removal
Curse and disease removal are straightforward paid services available directly from the guild’s Potion Shop (disease) and Wizard Shop (curses) — gold cost scales with the diagnosed severity tier, paid on the spot, no materials quest required. See Curse and Disease Removal for the full procedure and pricing reference.
Penalties
Roleplay-based consequences (reputation damage, NPC attitudes, obligations, restrictions on guild rank advancement) are welcome and encouraged. Avoid imposing strong mechanical disadvantages (persistent debuffs, stat penalties, loss of class features) as punishments.
Guild Progression
As the party accumulates successful contracts and reputation, they advance through guild ranks. Higher ranks unlock:

Access to more significant and better-paying contracts
More influential contacts within the guild and its network
Additional services or perquisites at the guild headquarters

Rank advancement should feel earned and meaningful. The DM should tie rank milestones to session achievements rather than a fixed XP threshold.
World & Lore
The Guild Headquarters
The party’s home base is the Faerûn Adventure League, headquartered in a self-sufficient castle complex in the outskirts of Waterdeep, on the Sword Coast.
See The Guild Headquarters for the full location note — services, shopping district, named NPCs, and notable features. Update that note (not this one) as the castle is explored further.
Known Factions, Locations, and NPCs
(None established yet — update after each session.)
Player Characters
The campaign uses a rotating Dungeon Master arrangement. All 5 players have a character; 3–4 are active in any given session while 1 runs the adventure.















































Character NameRaceClass / SubclassPlayerBackstory HooksLady CordeliaHumanRogue / Misfortune BringerTim StarLady Cordelia Ashworth was born into a wealthy noble family and raised with every luxury money could buy. After becoming a little too enthusiastic with her parents’ gold, she was formally cut off from the family fortune. To earn her way back in, Cordelia is now contractually required to complete a set amount of community service and learn what it means to hold an actual job. Naturally, she decided the most sensible—and dramatic—option was to join the Adventurers’ League. Cordelia believes she is completely unqualified for ordinary life, never realising that her noble upbringing has already given her valuable skills in combat, diplomacy, performance, etiquette, and manipulation. Her heart is usually in the right place, but her sheltered assumptions, blunt observations, and complete lack of awareness about how other people live mean that her attempts to help are not always appreciated.RookHalflingWarlock / ArchfeyTim Amos (Fro)Rook is an ordinary ferry runner who has come in sudden “good luck”. His good luck is actually an Archfey patron secretly steering him into a bigger story. The Archfey has taken on the appearance of a cat with wings who he has named as captain. (Appears as a normal cat to Rook who has taken them on as a pet)RindleGnomeArtificer / AlchemistMira DuncanRindle is a rugged alchemist who left his cosy tea shop to join the Adventurers’ Guild so he could act as a protective uncle to young, unprepared novices. He uses his guild status to safely harvest rare ingredients for his “Ultimate Comfort” potions—delicious, tea-flavoured elixirs meant to heal the weary—while sending his earnings home to support his struggling community.BrokOrcFighter / BattlemasterBrendon DuncanBrok grew up as a nomad in an orcish clan that prized strength but kept mostly to the wilds outside the cities — a safe, happy upbringing, with Brok never noticing the divide. While scouting near camp, he stumbled on a goblin merchant, Gallywinx, being shaken down by bandits — Brok’s approach alone sent them running. Impressed, Gallywinx hired him as a caravan guard: Brok’s presence kept trouble away without a fight, and Gallywinx, an outsider himself, paid him well and taught him an appraiser’s eye for goods. He can spot a fake gem in seconds, but reading a lying face is a skill Gallywinx never managed to teach him — and one he’s been burned by more than once. Genuinely fond of him, Gallywinx eventually pushed Brok toward the Adventurers’ Guild, hoping he’d build a name — and shift how the “lesser races” see orcs. Brok still keeps his armor polished to a mirror shine, a habit from Gallywinx and a point of real pride.DracoHumanRanger / HunterJames Reynolds—
One-Shots
One-shots are listed in play order. Read this list before generating a new one-shot to avoid repeating locations, villains, or major plot beats.

One-Shot 1 - One Giant Leap for Ratkin — A moonrat conspiracy to knock down the moon (believed to be cheese) climaxes during a lunar eclipse. City merchant job, warehouse theft, underground warren, rooftop climax.
One-Shot 2 - What Bramble Remembers — A dwarf wizard and his baby owlbear familiar. Necromantic soul-transfer. An undead owlbear that speaks in a dead man’s voice. Three endings, none easy.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Decoding the Scratched Walls
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Decoding the Scratched Walls
Act: 1–2 (bridges the transition)
Location: The Scratched Wall District
Encounter type: Exploration / Skill Challenge


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

Once you know to look, you see them everywhere — scratched low on walls, pressed into mortar between bricks, etched into the bases of market stalls. Always near ground level. Always in the same deliberate script. Some look ancient. Some look fresh. They’re everywhere in this district, and they form a pattern.


Setup
The symbol trail spans six blocks of the merchant quarter. The party must gather enough information to follow it to the warren entrance beneath the Coppergate Mill.
Skill Challenge: 4 successes before 3 failures.

Success: The party follows the trail cleanly to the entrance and has time to prepare before descending.
Failure (3 failures reached): The party eventually finds the entrance but makes enough noise that the warren is alerted. Guards inside have advantage on their first Perception check during Into the Warren.

Skill Challenge Checks


















































SkillDCContributionInvestigation12Recognise the symbols encode direction — a chevron motif always points toward the next clusterInvestigation15Spot that the trail doubled back twice, rerouted around a building constructed after the original path was laidNature12Fresh paw prints in the gutter follow the same route the symbols describeHistory14The oldest symbols use a noticeably different stroke style — at least three or four distinct “generations” of authorsPerception11A rat on a nearby rooftop is watching the party and retreats when noticedPersuasion13Talk Sergeant Wenda Brix into sharing the city guard’s full map of symbol sightings (counts as 2 successes)Arcana13Some symbols glow faintly under Detect Magic — a preservation enchantment keeps them from weatheringThieves’ Tools13Analysing the entry holes found throughout the district links them all to the same set of authors
Objectives
Find the warren entrance: a drainage tunnel beneath the Coppergate Mill, recently widened to roughly dinner-plate diameter. Large races (Medium or bigger) must succeed on a DC 10 Athletics check or spend 5 minutes widening it further to squeeze through.


                  
                  Scaling 
                  
                

If the party hits 2 failures and is struggling, have Sergeant Wenda Brix appear unprompted and offer her map — she’s been watching them and decides to trust them. Reset the failure count to 1.




                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

The moment a player realises “these are breadcrumbs left by intelligent rats” is a great table moment — pause on it, let it land, then confirm it with the Nature check showing fresh paw prints alongside decades-old symbols. Play up the absurdity: the symbols are right there at ankle height, all over a busy market district, and nobody has ever looked down.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Thane's Import House Investigation
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Thane’s Import House Investigation
Act: 1
Location: Thane’s Import House
Encounter type: Exploration


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The warehouse smells of sawdust and rope hemp — or it did, before most of the rope and lumber vanished. The remaining stock sits in disarray, as though carefully sorted through. Three ragged holes punch through the lower wall, each roughly the size of a dinner plate, edges chewed through brick. Near each hole, small precise marks are scratched into the mortar.


Setup
Thane’s warehouse was robbed over three consecutive nights. Entry points are unmistakably rodent-made (chewed brick) but large enough to haul significant material through, suggesting organisation and numbers. Nothing of obvious monetary value was taken — only hemp rope (30 metres), copper wire (a significant spool), and timber planks (a dozen). A character with a military or carpentry background will recognise this as exactly the material list for a large siege frame.
The symbols near the holes are small but precise — clearly a deliberate system, not random scratching.
Aldric Thane follows the party around describing the missing stock in exhaustive detail. Let him become background noise.
Discoveries








































CheckDCResultInvestigation10Entry holes were made from outside; drag marks show material was hauled outward into the alleyInvestigation13The symbols near each hole are in slightly different styles — as if made by different authors at different timesNature11Rat droppings and fur caught in the chewed edges. Definitely rats. Very large, organised rats.Nature14Fresh paw prints in the alley dust lead directly toward the drainage grate in the alley floorHistory15Rope, copper wire, and timber planks in these quantities suggest a tension-frame siege weapon — a ballista or similarArcana14One set of symbols carries a faint residual transmutation signature, as if something magically enhanced was briefly stored nearby
Objectives

Confirm the culprits are rats (or at least rodents)
Find the symbols and recognise them as a deliberate system
Locate the drainage grate in the alley (the start of the trail leading to The Scratched Wall District)



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Let the party feel clever here. Even without the high-DC checks, the core facts — rats, symbols, drainage grate — should emerge from any thorough search. The History check about siege weapons is a satisfying payoff; consider letting any character with a military background or proficiency in Carpenter’s Tools make it at DC 12 instead.
Thane monologuing about “forty metres of prime hemp rope, Mistran-braided” while a party member crouches over rat prints is an excellent tonal beat. Play it straight.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Guild Contract
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Guild Contract
Act: 1
Location: The Gilded Hook
Encounter type: Social


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The Gilded Hook smells of boot leather and last night’s stew. Mira Copperwick leans across the contract desk with her usual expression — professional patience worn very thin — and slides a sealed envelope toward you. “Aldric Thane. Merchant. Warehouse robbery, no obvious culprit, strange markings at the scene. He’s waiting in the side room. Try not to let him talk for more than ten minutes or he’ll never stop.”


Setup
Mira Copperwick briefs the party on the contract terms: 50 gold on completion, 20 gold upfront for expenses. Aldric Thane is waiting in the side room and has already been here for an hour.
Thane is a nervous, moderately wealthy importer who deals in building materials. He is convinced this is a coordinated criminal ring targeting him specifically. He is embarrassed to admit the culprits might be rats.
NPC Goals
Mira Copperwick: Get this contract off her desk. She’ll share everything she has (which isn’t much) and redirect the party to Thane.
Aldric Thane: He wants his materials back and an explanation. He’ll attempt to accompany the party to his warehouse; Mira Copperwick will talk him out of this if the party doesn’t.
Possible Outcomes

Full debrief: The party leaves knowing the specific materials stolen (hemp rope, copper wire, timber planks), the warehouse location, that symbols were found at the scene, and that similar symbols have appeared elsewhere in the district.
Rushed debrief: The party gets the basics and misses that Thane mentioned “symbols near every hole — same as the ones on Whitaker Street.” This costs them one clue in Act 2 and increases the Decoding skill challenge DC by 1.

Key skill checks:

Insight DC 11 — Thane is hiding that he initially dismissed the symbols as gang tags. On a success, the party can press him and learn that the symbols appear at multiple different ages, some clearly old.
Persuasion DC 12 — Convince Thane to add a 10 gp personal bonus on top of the guild’s standard prepayment.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Thane's Import House
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Thane’s Import House


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

A solid two-storey warehouse near the eastern docks district. The ground floor is open storage — or was. Most of the lumber and rope stock is simply gone, leaving gaps in the racks and sawdust outlines on the floor. Three ragged holes punch through the lower wall, each roughly the size of a dinner plate, edges chewed through brick. Near each hole, small precise marks are scratched into the mortar.


Notable Features

The missing stock area: Other materials left completely untouched — only hemp rope, copper wire, and timber planks were taken, as if from a list.
The entry holes: Three in the lower wall, chewed through brick. Scratch marks visible around each. A cluster of small symbols is pressed into the mortar near every hole.
The alley behind: Visible through the holes — a drainage grate in the alley floor is slightly displaced, with disturbed dust around it.

Hidden Details

DC 10 — Investigation: Entry holes were made from outside; drag marks in the sawdust show material was hauled outward through them, not inward.
DC 13 — Investigation: The symbols near each hole are in slightly different styles and depths, suggesting multiple authors at different times.
DC 14 — Nature: Paw prints in the alley dust lead directly to the displaced drainage grate.
DC 15 — History: The combination of materials taken — rope, copper wire, and timber planks in these quantities — matches a ballista construction list.

Battle Map
Shape: Rectangle
Dimensions: 60 ft. × 40 ft. (12 × 8 squares)
Cover & Terrain:

Storage racks (remaining stock) — along the North wall and centre of room — Half cover; can be toppled (DC 13 Athletics, creates 10 ft. difficult terrain on fall line)
Entry holes — South wall, evenly spaced — too small for Medium creatures, exit points for Small creatures only
Main loading doors — West wall, centre — double doors, currently closed

Interactive Objects:

Storage racks — North wall and centre — can be toppled onto enemies (DC 13 Athletics as an action; target in adjacent square makes DC 13 Dexterity save or takes 2d6 bludgeoning and is Prone)
Drainage grate (alley, outside South wall) — leads to The Scratched Wall District trail; requires DC 10 Athletics to lift
Hanging pulley and rope — ceiling, centre — DC 12 Athletics to swing across the room, avoiding ground-level difficult terrain

Encounters Here

Thane’s Import House Investigation

Connected Locations

The Gilded Hook
The Scratched Wall District



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Aldric Thane will follow the party around the warehouse describing the missing stock in exhaustive detail. Let him become comfortable background noise — the comedy is in the contrast between his monologue about “forty metres of prime hemp rope, Mistran-braided” and the party crouching over rat prints.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Gilded Hook
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Gilded Hook


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The Gilded Hook occupies the ground floor of a three-storey building wedged between a tanner and a cartwright. Inside: the smell of boot leather and old stew, a noticeboard thick with pinned contracts, and a half-dozen adventurers in various states of preparation. Behind the contract desk, a half-elf woman is already looking at you with the expression of someone who has been interrupted eleven times this morning.


Notable Features

Contract noticeboard: Covered in job postings of varying urgency and legibility. The Thane job is pinned near the top, marked standard priority — no combat expected.
Side meeting room: A cramped space with a table, three chairs, and a window overlooking the alley. A stout, overdressed merchant has been sitting in here for an hour.
The bar: The Gilded Hook technically serves food and drink. The cook is indifferent and the ale is reliable.

Hidden Details

DC 14 — Perception (crouching, examining the contract desk): A Moonrat symbol is scratched into the underside of the desk’s front panel — the same script found at Thane’s warehouse. Mira Copperwick doesn’t know it’s there. The route once ran directly beneath the Gilded Hook.

Battle Map
Shape: Rectangle
Dimensions: 50 ft. × 40 ft. (10 × 8 squares)
Cover & Terrain:

Contract desk — along the North wall, centre — Half cover for anyone crouching behind it
Bar counter — along the South wall, full width — Half cover
Scattered tables and chairs — centre of room — Difficult terrain (can be shoved aside as a bonus action)
Side meeting room doorway — East wall, North corner — chokepoint, single-file entry

Interactive Objects:

Noticeboard — North wall, East of desk — can be torn down to scatter papers and create a distraction (no mechanical effect, good for flavour)
Bar stools — along South wall — can be thrown as improvised weapons (1d4 bludgeoning, 20 ft. range)
Side meeting room door — East wall — can be barred from inside (DC 14 Strength to break down)

Encounters Here

The Guild Contract

Connected Locations

Thane’s Import House



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Give this place a lived-in feel: background chatter, someone patching armour in the corner, Mira dealing with two things at once. The party should feel like this is a functional, slightly chaotic workplace they belong to. Combat here is unlikely but not impossible — if it happens, the other guild members clear out fast and Mira ducks behind the desk.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Scratched Wall District
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Scratched Wall District


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

Six blocks of the merchant quarter, seen with new eyes. The symbols are everywhere — pressed low into every wall at ankle height, consistent and deliberate. Some are barely visible, weathered over years. Some look fresh. The district hums with market-day traffic. Nobody is looking down.


Notable Features

The trail: Symbols appear every twenty to thirty feet along a winding route through streets, alleys, and a short stretch of open plaza, always staying close to walls and avoiding open ground.
The age variation: Visible to anyone who looks closely — some symbols are shallow and eroded, others crisp and dark, as if written by different hands across many years.
The convergence point: Every trail in the district eventually feeds into the same alley behind the Coppergate Mill, ending at a drainage grate in the floor.

Hidden Details

DC 12 — Investigation: The symbols encode direction — a recurring chevron motif always points toward the next cluster, forming a readable path.
DC 13 — Arcana: Some symbols glow faintly under Detect Magic, carrying a preservation enchantment that prevents weathering. Someone has been renewing this periodically.
DC 14 — History: The age variation suggests this system has been actively maintained and extended over at least thirty to forty years — far longer than any single vandal’s project.

Battle Map


                  
                  No fixed combat encounter occurs here — this is a skill challenge location spread across several city blocks. If combat does break out (e.g. the party is ambushed by a moonrat scout), use the alley section below as the mat layout. 
                  
                

Shape: L-shaped alley
Dimensions: 40 ft. × 10 ft. with a 20 ft. × 10 ft. perpendicular branch (total 12 × 2 + 4 × 2 squares)
Cover & Terrain:

Market stalls — North side of main alley, evenly spaced — Half cover behind stall counters
Stacked crates — East end of main alley — Three-quarters cover stack; can be shoved (DC 11 Athletics, creates 5 ft. difficult terrain)
Drainage grate — South end, centre — difficult terrain; can be opened as an action (DC 10 Athletics) to reveal the tunnel to The Great Warren

Interactive Objects:

Market stall awnings — North wall — can be cut loose (one slash with a slashing weapon) to drop canvas and obscure a 10 ft. square (Lightly Obscured until cleared)
Drainage grate — South end — opens to the warren tunnel; Small creatures can drop in as a bonus action, Medium creatures as an action

Encounters Here

Decoding the Scratched Walls

Connected Locations

Thane’s Import House
The Great Warren



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

The merchant quarter is busy — carts, shopkeepers, foot traffic. The symbols are right there at ankle height and nobody has ever looked down. Lean into the mundane-surreal contrast. The party will get odd looks from shopkeepers as they crouch in alleys examining brickwork. That’s correct.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Aldric Thane
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Aldric Thane
Role: Quest client / Merchant
Location: Thane’s Import House
Personality

Pompous in proportion to how embarrassed he is — bluster is his default defensive move
Detail-obsessed: will tell you the exact weight of missing rope if you let him
Genuinely anxious underneath the bluster; this isn’t the first strange thing he’s noticed and it worries him

Appearance
A stout man in his mid-forties, overdressed for a warehouse visit, with a copper merchant’s seal on his signet ring and sawdust on his boots anyway.
Motivation
Recover his materials (he won’t) and get an explanation (he will). He wants to maintain the fiction that this was “a sophisticated criminal operation” and not, in any meaningful sense, rats.
Secret
Three months ago, Thane’s nightwatchman quit after claiming he saw rats “walking upright and carrying a map” near the warehouse. Thane paid him severance and told no one. He’ll share this if the party makes him feel like it won’t be used against him (Persuasion DC 12, or automatically if the party has already confirmed rats are involved).

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Mira Copperwick
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Mira Copperwick
Role: Guild clerk / Contract issuer
Location: The Gilded Hook
Personality

Efficient to the point of curtness — says what needs to be said and nothing more
Has seen genuinely bizarre contracts before and is unfazed; her deadpan delivery makes absurd situations funnier
Quietly proud of the guild and invested in its reputation, though she’d never admit it

Appearance
A compact half-elf woman in her fifties with ink-stained fingers, reading glasses perpetually perched on her forehead, and the expression of someone who has been interrupted eleven times this morning.
Motivation
Keep the guild’s contract board moving and its members employed. She has enough information to be useful and the good sense to stay out of the field.
Secret
She recognised the symbols from Thane’s description immediately — she saw similar marks on the wall behind the guild’s own cellar years ago and dismissed them as animal scratching. She won’t mention this unless pressed directly (Persuasion DC 14 or Insight DC 12 to notice she’s holding something back). If the party finds this out, the guild’s cellar contains a faded but complete set of Moonrat waypoint symbols — the route once ran directly under the Gilded Hook.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Sergeant Wenda Brix
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Sergeant Wenda Brix
Role: Potential ally / City guard sergeant
Location: The Scratched Wall District
Personality

Pragmatic: doesn’t care who solves the problem, just that it gets solved
Mildly contemptuous of guild adventurers on principle, but warms up quickly if they prove useful
Quietly convinced something strange is going on; has been saying this to her superiors for weeks with no traction

Appearance
A broad-shouldered human woman in her late thirties, city guard tabard slightly too large for her, with a notepad tucked under one arm and the confident posture of someone who has broken up a lot of fights.
Motivation
She wants the graffiti explained and the neighbourhood quiet. If the party is making progress where she couldn’t, she’ll share her resources — the city guard’s symbol map and access to drainage system records — in exchange for being kept in the loop.
Secret
She found a fresh set of Moonrat symbols inside the guard barracks’ cellar two weeks ago. She cleaned them off before anyone else saw them. She hasn’t told anyone because she doesn’t know what to do with it — if she reports it, someone will ask how rats got past the guard post, and she doesn’t have a good answer.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Into the Warren
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Into the Warren
Act: 2
Location: The Great Warren
Encounter type: Combat


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The tunnel opens into a vaulted chamber that has no right to be under a city street. The walls are packed earth braced with salvaged timber — your timber, from the look of it. Lanterns made of repurposed bottle-glass cast amber light across dozens of burrow entrances, stacked sleeping nests, and a geography that suggests this place has been growing for a very long time. Rats scatter at your entrance. Most of them. Not all.


Setup
The party has entered the Great Warren’s outer ring. Six Moonrats are on guard — conditioned by generations of training to defend the warren even without eclipse-level intelligence.
Phase 1 — Outer Guard: Four Moonrats challenge the party near the entrance. They fight as a pack, prioritising the same target. They will not pursue beyond the central corridor.
Phase 2 — Archive Guard: Two Moonrat Sappers guard the entrance to the Great Archive. They are smarter than average rats and use hit-and-run tactics — bite and duck into burrow holes, forcing the party to deal with uncertain positioning.
A brief lull between phases gives the party time to read archive wall carvings before engaging the sappers. Don’t skip this moment — it lands better mid-adventure than after combat ends.

Give the players time to read the archive walls between combat phases. Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Great Warren
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Great Warren


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

Beyond the drainage tunnel, the earth opens into something that has no right to be under a city street. The ceiling sits three feet high in most places. Salvaged timber shores up the walls. Bottle-glass lanterns cast amber light across sleeping nests, food stores, and a network of burrow-tubes running in every direction. On every surface, scratched in careful lines — text. Generations of it.


Notable Features

The outer chambers: Sleeping and eating areas. Dozens of ordinary rats scatter immediately at the party’s entrance.
The Great Archive: A larger chamber where every surface is covered in cramped but legible Common scratch-script. Notable sections: “On the Nature of the Cheese Moon (First Principles)”, “The Great Lunar Survey of Nibblefang XII”, “Ballista Construction Notes — Generations 23 through 41”, and “The Sacred Trajectory Calculations.”
The construction chamber: Where the ballista was assembled, then disassembled for transport to the roof. Empty now except for sawdust and copper wire scraps.

Hidden Details

DC 11 — Investigation (archive walls): An etched calendar marks every lunar eclipse for the past sixty years, with notes on what was accomplished during each one.
DC 13 — History (construction notes): The ballista design evolved across at least eight eclipse cycles over four decades — each generation inherited and improved the last iteration’s work.
DC 14 — Investigation (archive entrance): A small glyph near the archive doorway is a persistent alarm spell. DM’s discretion whether it already fired when the party entered.
DC 12 — Perception (archive, far wall): A section of wall is slightly different in texture — a sealed niche. Contains the Moonrat Treasure Hoard (see Into the Warren).

Battle Map
Shape: Irregular (two connected chambers with a narrow corridor between them)
Dimensions: Outer chamber 30 ft. × 25 ft. (6 × 5 squares); corridor 10 ft. × 10 ft. (2 × 2 squares); Archive chamber 35 ft. × 25 ft. (7 × 5 squares)
Cover & Terrain:

Timber support columns — outer chamber, evenly spaced in a 2 × 2 grid — Half cover; cannot be moved
Burrow holes — throughout all walls at ground level, every 10 ft. — impassable to Medium or larger creatures; Small creatures enter/exit as a bonus action
Sleeping nest mounds — outer chamber, South side — Difficult terrain
Archive wall carvings — Archive chamber, all walls — no mechanical effect; dense text provides flavour interaction
Bottle-glass lanterns — hung at head height every 15 ft. — AC 10, 1 HP; shattering one plunges a 10 ft. radius into darkness

Interactive Objects:

Timber support columns — outer chamber — can be used as half cover; cannot be toppled (load-bearing)
Bottle-glass lanterns — throughout — can be smashed (bonus action if adjacent) to create darkness in a 10 ft. radius
Sealed niche (archive, West wall) — DC 12 Perception to locate; contains the Moonrat Treasure Hoard

Encounters Here

Into the Warren

Connected Locations

The Scratched Wall District
Rooftop of the Coppergate Mill



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

The ceiling is 3 ft. high throughout — Medium creatures are effectively crouching the entire time, which halves movement speed unless the DM handwaves it for playability. Consider calling it out once for atmosphere and then ignoring the movement penalty so combat doesn’t grind. The cramped ceiling is a vibe, not a mechanic.
Give the party time to read the archive walls between combat phases. The Cheese Moon Doctrine is absurd and oddly moving — generations of rats, each with only a few hours of true intelligence across their entire lives, dedicating every one of those hours to this one goal. A party that reads feels the weight of it going into Act 3.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Rooftop Reckoning
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Rooftop Reckoning
Act: 3
Location: Rooftop of the Coppergate Mill
Encounter type: Combat / Social


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The mill roof is flat and wide, with a clear line of sight east across the rooftops to the open sky. At the centre stands a ballista assembled from rope and timber — elegant in a brutal, functional way. Around it, three rats work in hurried, purposeful silence.
Then the shadow crosses the moon. The eclipse begins.
The still rat at the front straightens. Adjusts a tiny sash. Turns to look at you with bright, sharp eyes.
“Ah,” says the rat, in perfectly clear Common. “The guild sent professionals. I respect that. But I’m afraid you’re too late to stop history.”


Setup
The eclipse has begun. Three Moonrat Sappers are loading and aiming the ballista. Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII is fully lucid and immediately opens diplomatic relations — he wants to explain, justify, and if possible, recruit the party to witness history.
The ballista fires in 3 rounds from the party’s arrival (the Sappers started early). On Round 3, it fires unless stopped.
The Eclipse: Lasts approximately 10 minutes of in-game time. When it ends, the Grand Squeaker loses all intelligence and language mid-sentence.
Enemies

  Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII
  Small beast, unaligned
  
  Armor Class 13
  Hit Points 22 (5d6 + 5)
  Speed 30 ft., burrow 15 ft., climb 30 ft.
  
  
    
      
        STR
        DEX
        CON

        16 (+3)

  Skills Arcana +6, Persuasion +5, Stealth +5
  Senses darkvision 60 ft., passive Perception 12
  Languages Common, Undercommon
  Challenge 1
  
  Eclipse Intelligence. While a lunar eclipse is active, the Grand Squeaker's Intelligence is 18 and it speaks Common and Undercommon. When the eclipse ends, its Intelligence returns to 2, it loses all languages, and all traits marked (Eclipse Only) cease to function.
  Keen Smell. The Grand Squeaker has advantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on smell.
  Tactical Genius (Eclipse Only). Moonrat allies within 30 feet of the Grand Squeaker have a +1 bonus to attack rolls.
  Actions
  Bite. Melee Attack Roll: +5, reach 5 ft. Hit: 6 (1d6 + 3) piercing damage.
  Rally the Warren (Eclipse Only, Recharge 5–6). The Grand Squeaker lets out a commanding squeak. Up to 3 Moonrats within 60 feet can use their reaction to move up to their speed.


Stopping the Ballista
Method 1 — Sabotage: A character adjacent to the ballista can attempt a DC 13 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) or Intelligence (Tinker’s Tools) check to damage the firing mechanism as an action. On a success, the ballista is disabled. On a failure, a Sapper notices and abandons loading to defend it.
Method 2 — Destroy it: Ballista AC 12, HP 18. Sappers actively defend it once it is attacked.
Method 3 — Negotiate a delay: Convince Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII to hear the party’s full case before firing. Persuasion DC 14 — on a success, Nibblefang grants one additional round of discussion per point above the DC. This does not stop the eclipse timer.
Method 4 — Disprove the Cheese Moon: Persuasion DC 20 (or DC 15 with extraordinary physical evidence, such as a fragment of actual moon rock). Almost certainly not available to the party, but worth noting for creative solutions.
Method 5 — Stall until eclipse ends: If the party keeps Nibblefang talking long enough, the eclipse ends mid-sentence and the Sappers stop working. The vibe, not hard mechanics, determines when this happens.
Nibblefang’s Arguments
Nibblefang has prepared for every objection. He is wrong, but not easy to beat:

“The moon is made of rock.” → “A rock that reflects light with such perfect, luminous warmth? Absurd. That is the glow of aged gouda.”
“A ballista bolt can’t reach the moon.” → “Forty-two generations of engineers disagree. The trajectory is flawless.”
“The bolt will just fall back down and hit someone.” → (He hasn’t considered this. DC 11 Insight reveals a flicker of doubt — push it. This is the crack in his certainty.)

Key skill checks:

Persuasion DC 14 — delay firing by 1 round per point of success margin
Persuasion DC 20 / DC 15 with evidence — convince Nibblefang the moon isn’t cheese
Insight DC 11 — identify which argument is landing
Insight DC 14 — sense the grief beneath his conviction; he knows this may be the Order’s last chance
Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) DC 13 — sabotage the firing mechanism

Possible Outcomes

Ballista disabled before firing: Full victory. See One-Shot 1 - One Giant Leap for Ratkin Possible Endings.
Ballista fires but falls short: Partial victory (party damaged it enough). The bolt splashes into the river. Thane is grumpy. See Possible Endings.
Ballista fires and strikes the moon: The bolt bounces off. The moon is rock. Nibblefang weeps. See Possible Endings.
Eclipse ends mid-encounter: Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII blinks, looks around blankly, and wanders toward the drainpipe. The Sappers stop working. Ordinary rats, ordinary night.



                  
                  Scaling 
                  
                

Easier: Reduce Sappers to 2; Grand Squeaker does not use Tactical Genius unless directly attacked. Harder: Add a 4th Sapper; the ballista fires in 2 rounds instead of 3.




                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

This encounter works best as a hybrid — let the party split their effort, one person talking to Nibblefang while others deal with the ballista. Don’t force a binary “fight or talk” choice. The funniest and most memorable runs have both happening simultaneously.
End the eclipse when the moment is most satisfying, not on a round count. Mid-sentence is ideal. “And so, at last, the Great Wheel of Gouda descends to — ” blink sniff wanders away.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Rooftop of the Coppergate Mill
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Rooftop of the Coppergate Mill


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The mill roof is flat and wide — the highest point in this part of the district, with a clear line of sight east across the rooftops to the open sky. Tonight, the moon is full and bright. At the centre of the roof stands a ballista assembled from rope and timber, elegant in a brutal and functional way. Three rats work around it in urgent, purposeful silence.
Above, the shadow is already crossing the moon. The eclipse has begun.


Notable Features

The ballista: Assembled from Thane’s stolen materials. Aimed directly at the moon, bolt loaded and ready. AC 12, HP 18. Fires in 3 rounds from the party’s arrival unless stopped.
The rooftop edge: A 2-foot parapet around the perimeter. Falling deals 3d6 bludgeoning damage (30-foot drop). Counts as difficult terrain when combat is near the edge.
The millstone access hatch: The only entry from inside the mill. Steep stairs, small hatch — Medium creatures must succeed on a DC 10 Dexterity saving throw or stumble onto the roof.
The copper sash: Worn across Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII’s chest. Fraying, repaired countless times, worn by forty-one predecessors. Worth nothing in gold; everything to the Moonrat Order.

Hidden Details

DC 12 — Perception: A fuse cord runs from the ballista’s trigger along the North parapet to the North-East corner — a remote-fire contingency the Sappers prepared in case they needed to clear the area.
DC 14 — Investigation (ballista): The aim is calculable. On a success, the character can determine exactly where the bolt will land if fired, and roughly where it would arc back down if it misses the moon.

Battle Map
Shape: Rectangle with 2 ft. parapet on all sides
Dimensions: 50 ft. × 40 ft. (10 × 8 squares)
Cover & Terrain:

Parapet wall — all four edges, 5 ft. wide — Half cover for creatures crouching behind it; standing on the parapet requires a DC 10 Acrobatics check or fall prone
Ballista frame — centre of roof, 10 ft. × 5 ft. — Three-quarters cover for creatures sheltering behind it; AC 12, HP 18
Access hatch — South wall, centre — difficult terrain; a creature entering from below must spend 10 ft. of movement to climb through
Fuse cord — runs along the North parapet from the ballista to the North-East corner — can be cut (any slashing weapon, no check required) to disable the remote-fire mechanism

Interactive Objects:

Ballista — centre — can be sabotaged (DC 13 Dexterity/Sleight of Hand or Tinker’s Tools as an action) or destroyed (AC 12, HP 18); fires in 3 rounds if not stopped
Fuse cord — North parapet — cutting it prevents remote firing; does not disable the manual trigger
Parapet edge — all sides — a creature pushed to the edge makes a DC 12 Strength saving throw or falls 30 ft. to the alley below (3d6 bludgeoning)
Access hatch — South wall — can be barred from above (an action; DC 15 Strength to force open from below)

Encounters Here

Rooftop Reckoning

Connected Locations

The Great Warren



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Give the party a cinematic beat on arrival — the eclipse is happening, the moon is right there, the ballista is pointed at it. Let them take it in for a moment before Nibblefang speaks. The scale of the absurdity should land fully before the scene accelerates into chaos.
The parapet edge is the most dangerous terrain feature — Moonrat Sappers will try to use Rally or thrown debris to push PCs toward it. Make sure players can see the drop.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII
Role: Villain (sympathetic) / Eclipse-form boss
Location: Rooftop of the Coppergate Mill
Personality

During eclipse: measured, eloquent, deeply philosophical — a true believer who has spent his brief intelligent life in preparation for this moment; genuinely curious about the party and willing to argue; considers dismissing their objections beneath him
Outside eclipse: a rat — large, perhaps with slightly brighter eyes than usual, but a rat nonetheless

Appearance
A large grey rat, notably bigger than typical, with a small sash of braided copper wire worn across his chest — the ceremonial garb of the Grand Squeaker, passed down through forty-one predecessors and repaired so many times it’s more patch than original. During the eclipse, his posture changes: he stands slightly straighter, and his eyes hold a quality that doesn’t belong in an animal.
Motivation
Fulfil the sacred mission of the Moonrat Order: harvest the Great Cheese Moon. He believes utterly in this goal and will die for it. He has also thought about it very carefully and considers the party’s objections intellectually weak — he welcomes the debate.
In negotiation, Nibblefang will counter every argument:

“The moon is made of rock.” → “A rock that reflects light with such perfect, luminous warmth? Absurd. That is the glow of aged gouda.”
“A ballista bolt can’t reach the moon.” → “Forty-two generations of engineers disagree. The trajectory is flawless.”
“The bolt will just fall back down and hit someone.” → (He hasn’t considered this. Insight DC 11 reveals a flicker of doubt — press it.)

Secret
The 42 generations of Moonrat grand squeakers have each had, on average, four to six hours of total eclipse-intelligence across their entire lives. Nibblefang has spent every eclipse minute studying the archive and preparing for tonight. He knows, on some level, that if this fails, the next generation may never pick up the cause — there are fewer Moonrats now than in previous generations, and the Order is fading. This is the last real shot. He won’t say this, but a character who succeeds on a DC 14 Insight check during negotiation can sense it — there is grief beneath the conviction.
Stat Block
See Rooftop Reckoning for full eclipse-form stat block. Outside the eclipse, treat as a standard Moonrat (CR 1/8).

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: One-Shot 1 - One Giant Leap for Ratkin
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
One-Shot 1 - One Giant Leap for Ratkin
Premise
A lunar eclipse is hours away, and something is stirring in the merchant quarter. Specific supplies have gone missing from warehouses, and a trail of cryptic symbols has been scratched into walls across the district — marks that appear at wildly different ages, as if left by many hands over generations. The party has a contract to investigate. What they’ll find is a centuries-long rodent conspiracy, an underground city of true believers, and a ballista aimed at the moon — because the Moonrats are this close to bringing down the giant wheel of cheese in the sky.
Hook
The adventuring guild has received a complaint from Aldric Thane, a merchant whose import warehouse has been systematically stripped of rope, copper wire, and timber — only those materials, nothing of obvious value. Stranger still: whoever took them left symbols scratched near every entry point they used.
Alternative hooks:

A city guard contact (Sergeant Wenda Brix) asks the party to look into the graffiti plaguing the merchant quarter, which the city can’t spare resources to investigate.
A party member notices a rat watching them with unusual intensity — following them across rooftops — and decides to find out why.

Act 1 — The Rat Report
The party receives the contract at the guild and meets Aldric Thane, who is equal parts baffled and offended. Investigation of his warehouse reveals the robbery was conducted with unusual precision: entry points are small (rodent-sized), specific materials were taken, and symbols are scratched near each hole. Thane doesn’t believe it was rats. He is wrong.
Following the symbols outside leads into the merchant quarter proper. The marks aren’t random graffiti — they form a trail. The party must decode enough of the symbol system to follow it before dark.
Key scenes: The Guild Contract · Thane’s Import House Investigation · Decoding the Scratched Walls
Act 2 — The Warrens Below
The trail leads to an entrance beneath the Coppergate Mill: a brick tunnel, rodent-sized but recently widened. Inside, the Great Warren unfolds — an underground complex that clearly took decades to construct. Chambers include sleeping areas, a food cache, and most importantly: the Great Archive, where generations of Moonrat scholars have carved their history, plans, and the sacred Cheese Moon Doctrine into every available surface.
The party can piece together the full picture here. The eclipse is tonight. Their predecessors built most of the ballista over multiple eclipse cycles. Tonight’s cohort plans to fire it. The machine was hauled up to the Coppergate Mill roof in pieces the night before. Moonrat guards must be dealt with to get through. A hidden alcove in the archive contains the generational treasure hoard — trinkets and coins collected over centuries.
Key scenes: Into the Warren
Act 3 — Rooftop Reckoning
The eclipse begins. The party reaches the mill roof to find three Moonrat Sappers assembling the final components of the ballista while Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII — moments ago an ordinary rat — straightens up, adjusts a tiny sash, and begins addressing the party in flawless Common.
The party can fight, sabotage the ballista outright, or negotiate with Nibblefang, who is intelligent, eloquent, and completely wrong about the moon being cheese. The eclipse lasts about 10 minutes of in-game time. When it ends, the Grand Squeaker trails off mid-sentence and wanders toward a drainpipe, confused.
Climax: Rooftop Reckoning
Possible Endings

Full Victory: The party disables the ballista and either defeats or talks down the Moonrats before the eclipse ends. The merchant quarter is safe. Thane pays up. The moon remains intact.
Partial Victory: The ballista fires — but the party damaged it enough that the bolt falls short and lands in the river. No one is hurt. The eclipse ends and the rats disperse. Thane still pays, albeit grumpily, as his stolen materials are a total loss.
Pyrrhic: The ballista fires true. The bolt strikes the moon… and bounces off. The moon is made of rock. The Moonrats are devastated. The Grand Squeaker, mid-eclipse, weeps. The party may never let this session be forgotten.

Act 1 — The Rat Report

Locations: The Gilded Hook · Thane’s Import House · The Scratched Wall District
Encounters: The Guild Contract · Thane’s Import House Investigation · Decoding the Scratched Walls
NPCs: Mira Copperwick · Aldric Thane · Sergeant Wenda Brix

Act 2 — The Warrens Below

Locations: The Great Warren
Encounters: Into the Warren
NPCs: —

Act 3 — Rooftop Reckoning

Locations: Rooftop of the Coppergate Mill
Encounters: Rooftop Reckoning
NPCs: Grand Squeaker Nibblefang XLII

DM Notes
Pacing: This one-shot runs in roughly three hours. Act 1 (30–40 min), Act 2 (60–75 min including combat), Act 3 (30–40 min). Don’t let the symbol-decoding drag — give partial information after two successes so the party always feels progress.
The Eclipse Timer: Once the party reaches the rooftop, the eclipse begins. Track it loosely — end it when dramatically appropriate, not on a rigid round count. The moment it ends mid-Nibblefang-sentence is the payoff.
Grand Squeaker as a Social Encounter: Nibblefang is not evil. He is a genius rat who genuinely believes in the Cheese Moon and has devoted his brief intelligent life to this moment. He will listen to reason but will not accept “the moon is made of rock” without extraordinary evidence. He will argue philosophy. He will quote his ancestors. Lean into it.
Common Derailments:

Party tries to keep a moonrat as a pet: Sure — a normal rat is a normal rat 23 hours a day.
Party tries to collapse the warren: Too extensive to collapse quickly. It would take days of sustained effort.
Party waits out the eclipse rather than engaging: The ballista is already aimed and loaded. If the party does nothing, it fires. Nibblefang anticipated this and has a fuse mechanism on the trigger.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Dinner at Durgins
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Dinner at Durgins
Act: 1 — Act 1 - Hearth and Feathers
Location: Durgin’s Cottage
Encounter type: Social / Light Challenge


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The dwarf is already talking before the door is fully open. “Yes, yes, the disturbances — terribly sorry, a circle went sideways, I’ve been meaning to reseal it, come in, you look like you haven’t eaten since Waterdeep.” He steps aside. From behind his legs, something the size of a large dog barrels past him, stops, and stares at you with enormous amber eyes. It makes a sound like a satisfied barn owl. It has feathers. It has a beak. It has already identified Rindle’s pack as a point of interest.


Setup
The party’s introduction to Durgin and Bramble. The meal is real, the hospitality is genuine, and Durgin is exactly what he appears to be — a lonely wizard who enjoys company. This encounter has two beats: the social dinner, and a minor challenge when the containment circle destabilises mid-meal.
NPC Goals
Durgin: Wants the party to enjoy the food, feel welcome, and not look too closely at the workroom. He deflects questions about the Academium letter if found — “old bureaucratic business, nothing interesting.” He is genuinely glad they’re here.
Bramble: Wants food, attention, and Brok specifically, in that order.
Bramble Beats
Run as many as fit the table’s energy:

The heist: Bramble steals something from Rindle’s pack. Rindle may oppose with a contested Sleight of Hand (Bramble +4). Bramble has already committed before anyone notices the attempt is in progress.
The shadow: Bramble follows Brok in exact lockstep when Brok crosses the room. If Brok stops, Bramble stops. If Brok turns around, Bramble sits down and looks at the ceiling.
The chair incident: Bramble walks under Cordelia’s chair with insufficient spatial awareness and tips it. He immediately sits on her foot. This is his apology. He means it.
The boot: When chalk dust irritates Durgin’s eyes mid-conversation, Bramble disappears and returns with a boot from the bedroom. Durgin takes it gravely and sets it to one side. “He does this. I don’t know what it means either.”

The Circle Problem
Halfway through dinner, the workroom hums. Durgin sighs and sets down his fork. “That would be the circle. Would anyone mind? I need two anchor points while I redraw the centre inscription — it’s quick.”
Mechanics:

Durgin handles the inscription (no check required)
Two party members each make DC 12 Arcana to hold anchor points; one other member may Help to grant advantage
Success: Circle sealed; disturbances end; Durgin quietly, genuinely grateful
Failure (one missed check): Minor discharge — a jar shatters, one party member’s hair stands on end for the rest of the evening, a faint smell of burnt copper. Circle is still sealed. Durgin apologises for the hair.

NPC Goals (Durgin deflection)
If asked about the workroom notation:
“Old notation, nothing current — research from some years back. I do keep meaning to clean the floor. More vegetables?”
Insight DC 13: He changed the subject very smoothly. He has done this before.
Possible Outcomes

Warm exit: Party leaves genuinely charmed by Durgin and Bramble, no suspicion — they’ll be harder hit by Act 2
Curious exit: Party found the letter (DC 14) or caught Durgin’s deflection (Insight DC 13) — they have a thread but don’t know what it connects to
Suspicious exit: Party is specifically suspicious of Durgin but can’t articulate why — useful if a player wants to stay on guard



                  
                  Scaling 
                  
                

The circle problem is optional. If the social roleplay has fully captured the table, skip it or run it as flavour only — the circle pops on its own with a smell of burnt copper, Durgin winces, and dinner continues. The purpose of this scene is to make the party care about these two. Everything else is secondary.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Disturbances
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Disturbances
Act: 1 — Act 1 - Hearth and Feathers
Location: Millhaven Village
Encounter type: Exploration / Skill Challenge


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The village elder points toward the tree line without quite looking at it. “It started three weeks ago,” she says. “Small things. Then the goat. Last night I heard something like an owl, but too low, too slow. Comes from that direction.” She pauses. “There’s a wizard out there. He’s been out there for fifteen years and never caused any trouble.” Another pause. “Much trouble.”


Setup
The magical disturbances radiate from Durgin’s failed containment circle in his workroom. The skill challenge ends when the party reaches Durgin’s door — the disturbances are formally “resolved” during Dinner at Durgins when the party helps reseal the circle.
Objectives
Identify the source of the disturbances and assess whether it is dangerous.
Skill Challenge
3 successes before 2 failures. Each success earns information; failures introduce minor complications.



































CheckDCSuccessFailureArcana11The magic reads as containment-school spillover — structured, passive, not wildReading is muddy; something secondary is masking the sourceNature10Affected animals are physically unharmed; the magic is passive and non-predatoryA chicken startles and must be caught before Aldra notices (comic interlude, costs 1 minute)Investigation12Disturbance gradient points clearly north-east toward the cottageOne party member steps directly under the levitating goat and is briefly elevated (comic; no damage)Perception11The low owl-sound is directional — comes from inside the cottage, not from the woodNothing of note; no information gained
On 3 successes: Party arrives at Durgin’s door with a working theory — structured, probably unintentional, probably fixable.
On 2 failures: Party arrives uncertain; one disturbance (the goat, the weather vane) persists through dinner. Durgin is visibly relieved when they don’t specifically mention the circle notation — DC 13 Insight to catch this.
Possible Outcomes

Standard: Party identifies the source with confidence and arrives prepared to be helpful
With failures: Party arrives with suspicion they can’t quite justify; Durgin’s warmth reads as slightly too easy if they’re looking for it



                  
                  Scaling 
                  
                

This is a purely investigative encounter with no combat risk. If the party rushes through it, have Bramble erupt from behind Durgin’s legs the moment the door opens — the energy reset is immediate and effective.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Durgin's Cottage
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Durgin’s Cottage


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The cottage sits slightly apart from the village, backed against the tree line. It is comfortably cluttered from the outside in: window boxes overflowing with herbs, a cracked cauldron repurposed as a planter, three stacks of firewood that have toppled into each other and not been restacked. Warm light shows through the windows. Something inside makes a sound like a large, contented owl.


Notable Features

A workroom visible through the front window — chalk circles on the floor, shelves of glass jars, a large slate board covered in notation
A living area dominated by a very large armchair occupied by a very small owlbear (Bramble, asleep with his face pressed on the armrest)
A kitchen with an active fire and the smell of something actually good cooking
Durgin’s front door, unlocked, with a small wooden sign: EXPERIMENTS IN PROGRESS — knock anyway, I forget to answer

Hidden Details

DC 14 — Perception or Investigation (study, during dinner): A half-burned letter wedged under a stack of books on the study shelf. The Arcane Academium seal is visible on the remaining fragment, addressed to “D. Stonehew,” dated six weeks ago. The readable portion includes: “…failure to demonstrate viable animus transference by the 30th will result in immediate revocation of all research licenses and seizure of materials…” Rindle identifies the Academium seal automatically — no check required.
DC 16 — Arcana (workroom): The chalk circle is not a containment diagram. The notation is too complex — it reads as a two-stage transfer: source anchoring, then vessel release. A successful check identifies it as soul-magic, which the Academium heavily restricts.

Battle Map
Not a combat location. No map required for Act 1.
Act 3 note: The cottage becomes a crime scene in Act 3. Durgin’s body is seated in the ritual circle in the workroom. The far wall has a 10 ft. × 10 ft. hole torn outward from the inside. The chalk circle is burned black at its centre. Players arriving here before following the tracks into the Thornwood will find this.
Encounters Here

Dinner at Durgins

Connected Locations

Millhaven Village
The Thornwood



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

The DC 14 letter is the adventure’s critical hidden discovery. Don’t volunteer it — let players explore. If no one searches the study by the end of dinner, have Bramble knock something off a shelf in there and draw attention to the room. The DC 16 workroom check is a bonus for perceptive players; don’t redirect attention to it, and don’t confirm or deny what it means if asked — Durgin deflects (“old notation, nothing current”).

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Millhaven Village
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Millhaven Village


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The village is small enough that you can see from one end to the other without squinting.
