A dozen or so buildings cluster around a common, ringed by farmland on three sides and a dark wood to the north-east. The air smells of turned soil and something faintly electric, like the moment before a thunderstorm. A goat stands on the village green — six inches above the ground, rotating slowly, entirely untroubled by its situation.


Notable Features

A levitating goat, rotating lazily at knee height — any attempt to pull it down causes it to rise slightly higher before resettling
A weather vane above the inn pointing steadfastly south regardless of wind direction
A cat sitting outside the smithy staring at the smithy wall, hissing at nothing visible every three minutes
Aldra’s house, identifiable by the guild contract notice pinned to the door and a hand-lettered sign reading KNOCK LOUDLY

Hidden Details

DC 11 — Arcana: The magical disturbances follow a rough gradient — weakest near the village centre, strongest toward the tree line to the north-east, where a cottage is just visible through the undergrowth.
DC 13 — Nature: The levitating goat is not distressed and is in no danger. Whatever is affecting it is structured, probably not catastrophic, and almost certainly not intentional.

Battle Map
Not a combat location. No map required.
Encounters Here

The Disturbances

Connected Locations

Durgin’s Cottage



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Keep this section light and funny. The levitating goat is the party’s first impression — bewildering but not threatening. Players who immediately try to solve the goat problem (Arcana, Athletics, Animal Handling) should find it gently resistant to their efforts; it descends on its own about an hour later regardless. Aldra will explain it has been doing this on and off for three weeks.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Aldra
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Aldra
Role: Quest giver / Village elder
First appears: Act 1
Location: Millhaven Village
Personality

Practical and straightforward — she describes problems clearly and doesn’t embellish
Privately fond of Durgin despite her exasperation; she’s complained about him to every passing merchant for years but would never actually report him to the city
Slightly guilty about filing the guild contract; she hoped the party would fix whatever Durgin broke and leave quietly

Appearance
A stout woman in her sixties with calloused hands and a grey braid pinned under a wide-brimmed hat she wears in all weather.
Motivation
Aldra wants the disturbances to stop before the village loses another animal to the hovering problem. She does not want Durgin punished or removed — she wants him to be more careful.
Secret
Aldra knew Durgin was sick with grief about Bramble. A month ago she brought him a pie and found him crying over a pile of research notes. She didn’t ask what they said. She wishes she had.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Durgin Stonehew
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Durgin Stonehew
Role: Key NPC / Tragic figure
First appears: Act 1
Location: Durgin’s Cottage
Personality

Warm and immediately hospitable — he offers tea before he offers his name
Fussy about his research notes and his workshop, relaxed about everything else
Prone to trailing off mid-sentence when a thought catches him; picks it back up three minutes later without acknowledging the gap

Appearance
A stout dwarf in his mid-hundreds, chalk-dusted at all times, with a short silver beard knotted with a worn copper bead that Bramble chewed on as a kit.
Motivation
Durgin has known for weeks that Bramble is dying. Every other avenue closed — licenses revoked, materials unavailable, conventional magic inadequate. Animus transference was the only thing left that could work. He chose to give himself because it was his to give.
Secret
Durgin completed the transfer ritual the night before the party arrived in Millhaven. His body is already dead in the workroom by the time the party reaches Act 3. By the time the party meets him in Act 1, he has perhaps eighteen hours of lucidity remaining as the two souls settle into each other — but they won’t know this until Act 3. He does not tell them.
Bramble
Bramble is an eight-month-old owlbear — small enough to fit under a table, old enough to have opinions. His feathers are cream-brown, his beak is pale, and he has enormous round amber eyes that he deploys strategically when he wants food. He treats Durgin as a climbing frame and the party immediately as potential friends.
Bramble’s behaviours in Act 1:

Steals something from Rindle’s pack (Rindle may oppose with a contested Sleight of Hand — Bramble has +4, and he has already committed before anyone notices)
Follows Brok in exact lockstep when Brok moves across the room, convinced this is a game
Knocks over Cordelia’s chair by walking under it with insufficient spatial awareness; sits on her foot as an apology
Brings Durgin a boot when chalk dust irritates Durgin’s eyes — this is apparently a comfort gesture; Durgin accepts it and sets it carefully to one side

Bramble’s favourite toy is a small carved wooden owl, worn smooth by months of chewing. It is left on the workbench beside Durgin’s open journal in Act 2.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Failed Experiments
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Failed Experiments
Act: 2 — Act 2 - The Weight of the Work
Location: The Thornwood
Encounter type: Exploration


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

In a hollow between two fallen trunks, you find them: a rabbit, a fox, a crow. All three are alive. All three are looking at you. The crow is perched on the fox. The rabbit is sitting inside the curve of the fox’s forepaw. Neither the fox nor the rabbit reacts to this. When you come closer, all three turn their heads to look at you at the same time, at the same speed, in the same direction.


Setup
These are Durgin’s early failed experiments — attempts to practice animus transference on small animals before committing to the full procedure. The failures didn’t kill the subjects; they produced a partial state where the transfer didn’t complete, leaving multiple creatures sharing a single set of responses. They are not in pain. They are not dangerous. They are very wrong.
Objectives
Understand what the party is looking at. No combat required or recommended.
Investigation






























CheckDCInformationArcana13Residual soul-magic in and around the animals — a transfer was attempted but didn’t fully complete. Two or more spiritual signatures occupying one body, or multiple bodies responding as one distributed awareness.Medicine12Physically healthy. Whatever is happening to them is metaphysical, not physiological. Their bodies are fine.Nature11These animals would not normally be near each other. Something drew them here, or they stayed after the procedure rather than dispersing.Insight14The animals are waiting for something. They are not afraid. They are also not entirely present — as though part of their awareness is elsewhere.
Possible Outcomes

Party understands they are looking at failed soul-magic experiments before they reach the cottage
Party does not understand what they are looking at until they read the journal; seeing this scene again in memory after the journal will hit differently



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Do not overplay this scene. It should be quietly disturbing, not horrifying. If players try to help the animals, they can’t — no spell available to level 3 characters addresses this. A DC 15 Arcana check tells them the state may resolve on its own over time, or may not. Let the party sit with that and move on when ready.
If players harmed the animals in the hollow — Durgin will know when the party meets him in Act 3. He’ll mention it. Not angrily. Just: “The animals in the hollow. I know what you found. I hoped they’d disperse.” This is a minor character beat, not a mechanical consequence. But it will land.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Empty Cottage
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Empty Cottage
Act: 2 — Act 2 - The Weight of the Work
Location: Durgin’s Cottage
Encounter type: Exploration / Roleplay


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The cottage door is ajar. The fire is out. When you push it open, the first thing you notice is the cold — and then the hole in the far wall of the workroom, jagged and outward-facing, large enough for something substantial to have passed through. The chalk circle on the floor is burned black at the centre. Durgin’s workbench is clear except for two things: an open journal, and a small carved wooden owl, worn smooth and slightly damp, as if someone held it very recently.


Setup
This is the emotional turning point of the adventure. There is no enemy here, no skill check required to understand what happened. The party finds Durgin’s body and reads his journal. This scene should run slowly.
What They Find
Durgin’s body is seated against the South wall inside the ritual circle, hands folded in his lap. He looks peaceful. A DC 11 Medicine check confirms he died within the past few hours — cardiac arrest consistent with extreme magical exertion. There are no marks on him.
Durgin’s journal lies open to the final entry. Players who page back through it find the full history. Rindle can read the research notes without a check. Other characters require DC 14 Arcana.
The Journal
Present each section as the party reads backward through the journal, or summarise for non-readers.


                  
                  Journal — Two Months Ago 
                  
                

Notes on Greyveil Wasting: a corruption of innate magical energy that manifests in creatures with arcane nature. No known cure. Progression: loss of coordination, loss of appetite, weakening of the innate magic that sustains the creature’s hybrid form. Terminal within three to four weeks of onset. Bramble is in the second week.
Correspondence with the Arcane Academium requesting a research waiver to pursue animus transference. Response: denied, pending review.




                  
                  Journal — Six Weeks Ago 
                  
                

Practice experiments on small animals in the Thornwood hollow. Partial results only — the transfer requires a complete soul as the animating source; a fragment or partial signature won’t sustain a failing vessel. Three subjects in partial state, stable but unresolved. Notes this may be permanent.
Academium revocation notice received via courier. All materials and components seized. Research license suspended. Durgin’s note on this: “Well. That closes that.”




                  
                  Journal — Final Entry (last night) 
                  
                

“Bramble ate his dinner tonight. The wooden owl is on the bench — I didn’t tell him why I left it there. I think he knows, though. He’s smarter than people give him credit for. Most people are.”
“The transfer requires a complete soul. I have one. It’s mine to give. The Academium will call this reckless. They’ll be right. I’ve been reckless about exactly one thing in a hundred and forty years, and it’s this ridiculous, wonderful, impossible animal, and I find I don’t mind.”
“If it works — and I think it will work — I’ll be in there somewhere. I expect Bramble will be in there too. I don’t know what that will feel like. I expect it will feel like him. I’m all right with that.”
“If the guild adventurers come back looking for me: they were very good company. Tell them I’m sorry about the contract fee.”


PC Hooks
Rindle: He reads the research notes and understands what they mean before he finishes the first page. He will be the one who has to explain the mechanics to the rest of the party. This is not a comfortable thing to have to do.
Lady Cordelia: The Ashworth name appears mid-journal — the Ashworths donated to the Academium three generations ago, granting historical first-claim rights over research conducted under their patronage. Cordelia may recognise the legal implication or simply feel a complicated guilt-by-association. Either is valid.
Possible Outcomes

Party reads the journal fully and understands what happened; they follow the tracks
A party member may need a moment before they’re ready to move. Allow it.



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

If players try to help Durgin here — Spare the Dying, Healing Word, anything at all — let them try. None of it works. He’s been gone for hours. Then give them the journal.
The wooden owl should be mentioned specifically when describing the workbench. Players who remember Bramble carrying it during Act 1 will understand what its presence on the bench means.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Thornwood
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Thornwood


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The trees here are old and close together — not a managed wood but a place that has been left entirely to its own devices. The undergrowth is dense at the edges and thins toward the interior, where the canopy blocks enough light that nothing grows from the floor. It is quiet in the specific way places get when animals have decided to be somewhere else.


Notable Features

Tracks in the soft ground near the cottage’s torn wall — initially large but irregular, as if whatever made them was finding its footing
A cleared hollow 200 ft. north of the cottage where bark has been stripped from several trees at roughly six feet of height, in parallel lines
A cold spot approximately halfway into the wood — temperature drops noticeably without wind or shade to explain it
A faint blue-grey light visible deeper in, when viewed from the hollow at night

Hidden Details

DC 12 — Survival: The tracks belong to something significantly larger than Bramble — four-legged, heavy, with a gait pattern unlike a normal owlbear. Or something that was recently much smaller.
DC 14 — Investigation (stripped bark): The claw marks follow a repeated pattern, not random damage. Something was testing its reach and strength. Methodically.
DC 15 — Arcana (cold spot): Residual necrotic energy, recent. Not dangerous at this concentration, but significant — whatever happened nearby involved soul-magic of considerable complexity, completed within the past twelve hours.

Battle Map
Shape: Irregular woodland (traversal zone)
Dimensions: Variable — use the full play area; the Thornwood is a pressure ramp between investigation and confrontation, not a fixed combat space
Cover & Terrain:

Dense undergrowth — South and East edges — Difficult terrain for first 20 ft. from the cottage side
Old-growth trunks — scattered throughout — Half cover; Large or smaller creatures can break line of sight by moving to the opposite side
Root systems — throughout — Difficult terrain in clusters; DC 10 Acrobatics to move at full speed across roots in dim light

Encounters Here

Failed Experiments
What Bramble Remembers

Connected Locations

Durgin’s Cottage
The Binding Glade



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

The Thornwood is a pressure ramp — it should feel like walking toward something the party isn’t sure they want to find. Describe the cold spot and the stripped bark as separate discoveries at separate moments. The blue-grey light visible from the hollow is the Binding Glade. Let players see it and choose to move toward it. That choice is important.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: What Bramble Remembers
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
What Bramble Remembers
Act: 3 — Act 3 - What Bramble Remembers
Location: The Binding Glade
Encounter type: Social (Combat optional)


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The sound comes first — low, somewhere between an owl and a moan, too structured for wind. Then you see it step from the north tree line: the size of a draft horse, four-legged, frost-rimed, with pale grey eyes that cast their own faint light. Its feathers are dark where they should be cream-brown. It is breathing, but its breath doesn’t fog in the cold air.
It stops when it sees you. It does not move.
A long moment. Then:
“…you came back.”
Durgin’s voice. Slower than you remember. From somewhere inside the creature.
“I had to see if you would.”


Setup
The undead owlbear — Durgin-Bramble — stands at the north tree line and waits. It will not approach unless the party indicates they want it to. It is not aggressive. Bramble’s instincts surface occasionally (the head tilts; a low sound; brief fixation on something in the dark before Durgin pulls attention back), but Durgin is present and coherent. He has perhaps an hour of lucidity remaining before the two souls blur together fully.
Pause after the reveal. Give the table a moment before Durgin speaks again. Let them react. Then:
“I know what this looks like. I know. I’m sorry about the wall.”
What Durgin Can Say
He is warm, apologetic, and quietly wry about his situation. He is at peace with what he did. He is not at peace with the fact that the party is upset.

“The research notes were in the journal. I trust you read them. I hope Rindle explained the technical parts — I know I write in shorthand.”
“I can feel him in here. It’s — it’s like remembering something at the same time you’re being reminded of it. Does that make sense? It probably doesn’t.”
“Bramble remembers all of you. Specifically — Brok, he’s very fixated on Brok, I don’t know what you did but he thinks very highly of you.”
“I don’t have a lot of time before — before it becomes more him than me. I’d like to say goodbye properly, if that’s all right.”
(If asked about the Academium): “They’ll come, probably. They tracked the ritual signature. I expect they’re already on their way.”

Velthrane’s Arrival
Magistra Velthrane arrives with two Academium Sentinels approximately 10 minutes after the party first speaks with Durgin-Bramble — from the east tree line. She takes in the scene and addresses the party rather than the creature:
“The creature is Academium property under the Research Seizure Act. I am prepared to offer formal documentation and a finder’s compensation for its recovery. Please stand aside.”
Social DCs vs. Velthrane:






























ApproachDCNotesIntimidation14She has institutional backing and she knows itPersuasion (ethics)16She doesn’t disagree on ethics — she disagrees on jurisdictionPersuasion (Ashworth/Cordelia)10This genuinely throws her; she straightens her cuffs twiceDeception (timeline misdirection)15She is sharp, but can be misdirected about when the transfer completed
Ashworth gambit: If Cordelia invokes her family name and the historical donation, Velthrane’s composure cracks visibly. She asks for clarification. On success (DC 10 Persuasion), she agrees to defer to guild adjudication rather than press her claim tonight. She and the sentinels withdraw — “This isn’t over” — and the party has the glade to themselves.
Academium Sentinels (2)

































AC16 (chain mail and shield)HP26 (4d8 + 8)Speed30 ft.STR / DEX / CON15 / 12 / 14INT / WIS / CHA10 / 11 / 10CR1/2
Spear. Melee or Ranged Weapon Attack: +4 to hit, reach 5 ft. or range 20/60 ft. Hit: 5 (1d6 + 2) piercing damage.
Shield Bash. Melee Weapon Attack: +4 to hit, reach 5 ft. Hit: 4 (1d4 + 2) bludgeoning damage. The target must succeed on a DC 12 Strength saving throw or be knocked prone.
Tactics: Sentinels position between Velthrane and the party. They use Shield Bash to knock prone anyone moving toward her. They do not pursue fleeing party members and will disengage if Velthrane orders withdrawal.

Resolution Options
Mercy
Trigger: Durgin asks, or a party member asks on his behalf.
“I’d like to stop, I think. It was — it was worth doing. I don’t regret it. But I’m tired.”
Release ritual: One party member makes a DC 12 Arcana check. Other party members may Help (granting advantage). Durgin talks them through it — he knows exactly what is needed.

Success: The undead owlbear grows very still. Its pale eyes dim slowly. The chalk sigils on the ground flare once, bright, then go dark. The body settles. Both souls pass on.
Failure: Durgin’s voice grows quieter, then steadies — “Try again. Shift the anchor left — yes, there.” Automatic success on the retry. He compensates from inside.

If Velthrane is still present: She stands very still through the ritual and says nothing for a long moment after. Then: “I’ll note in my report that the transfer was verified successful.” She and the sentinels leave without further comment.
Durgin’s last words (Mercy): “Thank you for the company.”

Reversal
Trigger: The party attempts to separate the souls rather than release them.
“It might work. I don’t — I don’t know what it would mean for Bramble. For either of us. I think you should try, if you want to try.”
Ritual: DC 17 Arcana check, group effort — all willing party members make the check each round. Requires three successes before two failures across all participants combined.

Success (3 before 2): The two signatures separate. Durgin’s soul detaches — coherent, at peace, speaking clearly through the process. He has time to say something specific to each party member present (DM discretion — something he noticed during dinner). Then the undead owlbear’s animation fails. It falls. Both Durgin and Bramble are gone. The party gets a proper goodbye.
Failure (2 before 3): Durgin’s voice stops mid-sentence on the second failure. The owlbear stands very still for a long moment. Then it turns and walks slowly into the dark Thornwood. Only Bramble’s animal instinct remains. He is alive — but Durgin is gone, without a goodbye.


Defiance
Trigger: The party fights off Velthrane’s guards (or bluffs/negotiates them away) and gives Durgin-Bramble a choice rather than making it for him.
“…I think I’d like to keep going for a while. There’s a lot I — Bramble always wanted to see more. He always wanted to see more of everything.”
The undead owlbear turns toward the deep Thornwood. It pauses at the tree line.
“Tell Aldra I’m sorry about the goat. I fixed the circle before I came out here. It should come down on its own.”
Then he goes.
The contract is technically unclosed. Aldra pays the second half of the reward regardless — “the disturbances stopped, didn’t they?” The guild closure note reads: “Disturbances resolved. Cause: experimental necromantic research, now concluded. Researcher status: unknown.”



                  
                  Scaling 
                  
                

If combat occurs (Velthrane + 2 sentinels vs. 3–4 level 3 players), it is a Deadly encounter. Durgin-Bramble will not fight for the party but will position itself between Velthrane and the party, blocking line of sight and forcing her to reposition — this effectively costs her one action per round.
At 4 players: Run as written. Velthrane opens with Hold Person on the most physically threatening character.
At 3 players: Remove one sentinel. Have Velthrane offer to negotiate after she takes any damage — she is not a martyr.




                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Whatever ending the players choose, end on Durgin’s voice. If Mercy: his last words as the light fades are “Thank you for the company.” If Reversal: during the ritual, he addresses each party member by name — something specific he noticed about them during dinner. If Defiance: he’s gone into the trees before the party thinks to say anything more. That’s fine. That’s the ending that hurts the right way.
After any ending: the glade is quiet. The chalk sigils are dark. The stars are still visible through the gap in the canopy. Give the table a moment before asking if they want to head back to Millhaven.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: The Binding Glade
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Binding Glade


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The trees open into a near-perfect circle, roughly sixty feet across. The canopy closes above it but doesn’t seal — you can see stars through a gap at the centre. The ground is scorched in a large spiral pattern, and the air smells of old copper and frost. Chalk marks trace the spiral outward to the clearing’s edge, worn but still legible, still faintly luminous. Four iron torch stakes stand at the compass points, burned down to nothing. It is very quiet. And then something moves in the trees to the north.


Notable Features

A scorched spiral at the clearing’s centre, 15 ft. across — the remains of the ritual circle, burned black at the core
Chalk sigils running outward from the spiral to the tree line, still faintly luminous in dim light
Temperature several degrees colder than the surrounding wood, with no wind to explain it
Four iron torch stakes at cardinal positions, burned to nothing — the iron itself is frost-rimed

Hidden Details

DC 12 — Arcana: The chalk sigils form a two-stage transfer diagram. The first stage anchors the source soul; the second releases it into the target vessel. Both stages completed successfully. This is not a failed experiment.
DC 15 — Arcana: Two distinct soul-signatures linger in the clearing, partially overlapping. Still present, still active — but not fully integrated. The boundary between them is blurring.
DC 10 — Perception (after the reveal): The undead owlbear’s breath does not fog in the cold air. Its eyes do not blink at normal intervals. Its body radiates no warmth.

Battle Map
Shape: Circular
Dimensions: 60 ft. diameter (12 × 12 squares)
Cover & Terrain:

Tree line — runs around the full perimeter — Full cover beyond; half cover at the edge for Large or smaller creatures
Scorched spiral — centre 15 ft. — Difficult terrain (cracked, raised edges); lightly obscured at ground level from residual smoke-haze
Iron torch stakes — North, South, East, and West, each 25 ft. from centre — No cover, but can be used as improvised clubs (+4 to hit, 1d4+2 bludgeoning) or driven as anchors (useful in the Mercy release ritual)

Interactive Objects:

Ritual chalk sigils — floor, centre to perimeter — Spending one action to study them grants advantage on Arcana checks to understand or attempt to reverse the binding
Iron torch stakes — North, South, East, West — Can be pulled from the ground (DC 12 Athletics) and used as improvised weapons or ritual anchors

Encounters Here

What Bramble Remembers

Connected Locations

The Thornwood



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

The glade should feel like a destination, not an arena. When the party first arrives, describe the emptiness before the sound. Give them a moment with the ritual circle — Rindle might crouch to read the sigils, someone might pick up a burned-out torch. The gap in the canopy and the stars above are important: this should feel like the world is watching. The reveal — Durgin-Bramble stepping from the north tree line — should feel like it has been coming since Act 1. Do not rush it.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Magistra Velthrane
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Magistra Velthrane
Role: Antagonist (negotiable)
First appears: Act 3
Location: The Binding Glade
Personality

Precise and formal — she speaks in the clipped cadence of someone who has spent decades writing institutional reports
Genuinely believes the Academium is right and Durgin was wrong; she’s not a villain, she’s an institution wearing a person’s face
Has a tell when she’s uncertain: she straightens her cuffs, one then the other, before responding

Appearance
A tall human woman in her fifties, silver-streaked dark hair pulled back severely, wearing Academium grey robes with the institutional seal embroidered at the collar in silver thread.
Motivation
Velthrane has been tracking Durgin’s research for six weeks. She does not want the creature harmed — she wants it studied. In her professional assessment, Durgin has produced the first confirmed animus transference in forty years, and losing access to the subject would be a genuine loss to the Academium’s understanding of soul-magic persistence. She is not wrong about the academic significance. She is wrong about everything else.
Secret
Velthrane was the one who denied Durgin’s research waiver six weeks ago. She flagged his application as reckless and forwarded it for rejection herself. She has not mentioned this to anyone and has not fully processed what it means that she effectively removed the legitimate avenue before he was forced to use himself. If the party pushes her on this — “you denied his waiver and then drove him to use himself as the subject” — she will not be able to maintain her composure.
Cordelia Hook
The Ashworth name stops Velthrane mid-sentence. The donation predates the current Academium charter and creates a historical patronage claim that pre-empts several of her procedural authorities. She has not encountered this legal situation before. She will ask for clarification — unusual for her — and may agree to defer to guild adjudication rather than press further.
Stat Block

  Magistra Velthrane
  Medium humanoid (human), lawful neutral
  
  Armor Class 13
  Hit Points 45 (10d8)
  Speed 30 ft.
  
  
    
      
        STR
        DEX
        CON
        INT
        WIS
        CHA
      
      
        9 (-1)
        12 (+1)
        11 (+0)
        17 (+3)
        14 (+2)
        13 (+1)
      
    
  
  
  Saving Throws Int +5, Wis +4
  Skills Arcana +5, History +5, Insight +4, Deception +3
  Senses passive Perception 12
  Languages Common, Elvish, Draconic
  Challenge 4
  
  Soul Sight. As a bonus action, Velthrane can detect the presence and approximate location of active soul-magic within 60 ft., including animated undead, bound spirits, and animus transfer effects. This is how she tracked the ritual.
  Spellcasting. Velthrane is a 7th-level spellcaster (Intelligence, spell save DC 13, +5 to hit with spell attacks). Cantrips (at will): Toll the Dead, Mage Hand. 1st level (4 slots): Shield, Detect Magic, Ray of Sickness. 2nd level (3 slots): Hold Person, Ray of Enfeeblement, Misty Step. 3rd level (3 slots): Counterspell, Vampiric Touch, Animate Dead.
  Actions
  Quarterstaff. Melee Weapon Attack: +1 to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 2 (1d6 - 1) bludgeoning damage.
  Toll the Dead. One creature within 60 ft. must succeed on a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw or take 1d12 necrotic damage (or 1d8 if the target is at its hit point maximum).
  Necrotic Lance (Recharge 5-6). Ranged Spell Attack: +5 to hit, range 90 ft., one target. Hit: 16 (3d10) necrotic damage.
  Reactions
  Shield. When hit by an attack, Velthrane casts Shield as a reaction, gaining +5 AC until the start of her next turn (potentially causing the triggering attack to miss). Uses a 1st-level spell slot.

Tactics
Velthrane prefers not to fight. If the party forces combat, she immediately casts Hold Person on the most physically threatening character and retreats behind her sentinels. She uses Necrotic Lance against anyone who moves toward her and Counterspell to deny high-level party abilities. She will attempt to flee rather than fight to the death — she is not paid enough to die in a forest clearing over a research specimen, and she knows it. If reduced to 15 HP or fewer, she calls for withdrawal and leaves.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: One-Shot 2 - What Bramble Remembers
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
One-Shot 2 - What Bramble Remembers
Premise
The party is contracted to investigate magical disturbances near Millhaven, a quiet farming village on the outskirts of Waterdeep. The source is Durgin Stonehew — a warmhearted dwarf wizard whose experimental research is leaking into the surrounding area. When the party meets him and his baby owlbear familiar, Bramble, everything seems manageable. It isn’t. Durgin has been hiding something that will outlast him.
Hook
The guild board carries a contract marked URGENT: “Millhaven residents report unexplained magical phenomena — levitating animals, reversed compasses, unexplained sounds after dark. Locals believe the old wizard on the village edge is responsible. Assess and resolve. Client: Aldra, village elder. Reward: 80gp upon resolution (40gp upfront).”
Alternative hooks:

Rindle recognises Millhaven as the source of a rare alchemical herb he’s been sourcing — his supplier wrote to him directly because the disturbances are disrupting the harvest.
Lady Cordelia’s family steward flagged an unusual complaint forwarded through the Ashworth estate’s old patronage network — someone in Millhaven is making noise about a wizard and it’s becoming embarrassing.
Brok’s caravan guard instincts were triggered by a merchant who passed through the guild that morning, spooked by something large he heard moving in the Thornwood at night.

Act 1 — Hearth and Feathers
The party arrives in Millhaven to find a village quietly losing its mind: a goat hovering six inches above the ground, a weather vane spinning backwards in still air, a cat staring at nothing and hissing. Aldra, the village elder, briefs them and pays the first half of the contract. Following the disturbances leads directly to Durgin’s cottage at the village edge — a warm, cluttered place that smells of pine resin and old books.
Durgin meets them at the door covered in chalk dust, immediately apologetic and cheerfully unfazed. He introduces Bramble, his eight-month-old baby owlbear, who barrels past Durgin’s legs to investigate the party. The disturbances are a minor problem — a containment circle failed in his workroom. With the party’s help, he seals it. He insists they stay for dinner.
Players who search the study during the meal may find a half-burned letter from Magistra Velthrane of the Arcane Academium.
Key scenes: The Disturbances, Dinner at Durgins
Act 2 — The Weight of the Work
Overnight, the disturbances change: colder, quieter, wrong in a way that is hard to name. Tracks at the cottage’s edge lead into the Thornwood. Following them reveals what Durgin has been practicing on — small animals with corrupted spiritual signatures, flickering between states. Unsettling, but not grotesque.
The cottage is empty when the party returns. Bramble is gone. The far wall has been torn outward from the inside. Durgin’s journal lies open on the workbench. Bramble’s favourite toy — a chewed wooden owl — sits beside it.
The journal tells the whole story: Bramble has Greyveil Wasting, a corruption of his innate owlbear magic that will kill him within weeks. Durgin spent months researching animus transference — a form of outlawed necromancy that moves an animating soul from one vessel to another. The Arcane Academium revoked his license when they found out, cutting off access to materials and components. Durgin’s final journal entry is dated the previous night.
Rindle can read Durgin’s research notes without an Arcana check. He will be the one who has to explain what they mean to the rest of the party. Cordelia finds her family name in the journal — the Ashworths donated to the Academium three generations ago, granting historical “first claim” rights over research conducted under their patronage.
Key scenes: Failed Experiments, The Empty Cottage
Act 3 — What Bramble Remembers
Heavy tracks lead deep into the Thornwood. The party follows them by torchlight until the trees thin into a clearing. A low sound reaches them first — somewhere between a hoot and a moan, too low for a bird, too structured for wind.
A large shape steps into the torchlight. The undead owlbear is frost-rimed, pale grey eyes glowing faintly. Larger than Bramble. Wrong in a way that is immediately apparent. It stops when it sees the party.
“…you came back.”
Durgin’s voice. From somewhere inside the creature.
“I had to see if you would.”
Magistra Velthrane arrives with two Academium guards shortly after, having tracked the ritual’s magical signature. She presents legal documentation and claims the creature as Academium property — the first confirmed successful animus transference in forty years. She is not immediately violent; she believes she has the authority. Cordelia is uniquely positioned to challenge this.
The resolution belongs to the players.
Climax: What Bramble Remembers
Possible Endings

Mercy: Durgin asks for rest. With the party’s help (DC 12 Arcana — Durgin guides them through it), a release ritual frees both souls. The owlbear’s body goes still. Two souls pass on together. Velthrane leaves with documentation but no specimen.
Reversal: The party attempts to separate the souls (DC 17 Arcana, group check, three successes before two failures). Success: Durgin’s soul passes on peacefully — a proper goodbye. The undead collapses. Failure: Durgin’s voice fades mid-sentence. The owlbear stands still, then walks into the dark. Only animal instinct remains.
Defiance: The party fights off Velthrane’s guards. Durgin-Bramble chooses the Thornwood. “I’d like to see a bit more of the world. Bramble always wanted to.” The contract goes unclosed.

Act 1 — Hearth and Feathers

Locations: Millhaven Village, Durgin’s Cottage
Encounters: The Disturbances, Dinner at Durgins
NPCs: Durgin Stonehew, Aldra

Act 2 — The Weight of the Work

Locations: The Thornwood
Encounters: Failed Experiments, The Empty Cottage
NPCs:

Act 3 — What Bramble Remembers

Locations: The Binding Glade
Encounters: What Bramble Remembers
NPCs: Magistra Velthrane

DM Notes
Pacing: Act 1 should feel warm and unhurried. Resist the urge to signal dread early — let the players genuinely enjoy Durgin and Bramble. The levity beats are not decoration; they are load-bearing. The harder the fall, the better the story.
The reveal: When Durgin-Bramble speaks for the first time, pause. Don’t rush to the next beat. Give the table a moment. If players immediately try to help or fight, let them — but Durgin will ask them to slow down first.
Velthrane’s arrival: She should arrive about 5–10 minutes (real time) after the party first speaks with Durgin-Bramble. Don’t let her arrival cut the emotional moment short — she can wait at the tree line.
If players attack Durgin-Bramble: The undead owlbear defends itself but does not pursue. Durgin’s voice becomes distressed: “Please — I don’t want to hurt you. I just wanted to see you again.” This should stop most parties.
The Cordelia hook: Velthrane will recognise the Ashworth name immediately. Her composure will crack, briefly. The Ashworth donation predates the current Academium charter — it is a genuine legal complication she did not anticipate.
Contract status: The contract (resolve the disturbances) was technically completed at the end of Act 1. Aldra pays the second half regardless of Act 3 outcomes. The guild closure note should read: “Disturbances resolved. Cause: experimental necromantic research, now concluded. Researcher deceased.”

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Curse and Disease Removal
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Curse and Disease Removal
This note defines the procedure when a character needs a curse or disease removed through guild services.
Trigger
This event activates when:

A character contracts a disease and seeks treatment at The Bubbling Cauldron (Potion Shop)
A character is cursed and seeks removal at Bilgo Bangwiz Bazaar (Wizard Shop)

Simple diseases or minor curses handled by low-level spell effects (e.g. Lesser Restoration) during a normal session do not trigger this procedure. This event is for conditions requiring the guild’s specialist services.
Procedure
Guild removal services are a straightforward paid transaction — no materials quest required.
1. Diagnosis. The relevant specialist (Aster for disease, Bilgo for curses) examines the character and identifies the severity tier of the condition.

Disease: Common / Rare / Exotic Magical (see The Bubbling Cauldron for pricing)
Curse: Basic / Powerful / Ancient or Legendary (see Bilgo Bangwiz Bazaar for pricing)

2. Payment. The party pays the listed gold cost for that severity tier, per the relevant shop’s price list.
3. Treatment. The condition is removed on payment. No materials collection, no dedicated one-shot.
Exception — Ancient/Legendary curses: Bilgo’s price list lists these as “consultation required” rather than a flat fee. At the DM’s discretion, a sufficiently severe or story-relevant curse in this tier can still escalate into a short quest or negotiation if it serves the session — but this is an optional narrative choice, not the default procedure.
Notes for the DM

Scale the severity tier to the narrative threat, not just flavor — a disease picked up from a minor scuffle should be Common, not Exotic.
Affordability is the pressure point, not a quest requirement. If the party can’t cover the cost, that’s a roleplay/financial complication (a loan from the guild, a favor owed, a discount negotiated) — consistent with the campaign’s resource-attrition difficulty design.
The condition remains active until paid for — this still gives the party a reason to prioritize it, just without forcing a session detour.



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

This procedure was updated to match the priced services established for The Bubbling Cauldron and Bilgo Bangwiz Bazaar — it previously required a dedicated materials-collection one-shot, but that’s been replaced with straight gold cost for consistency across DMs. If a particular curse or disease has strong story potential, nothing stops a DM from building a one-shot around its source anyway — just don’t make it a prerequisite for the cure.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Player Death
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Player Death
This note defines the procedure when a player character dies. The DM running the session is responsible for applying this consistently.
When Death Occurs
A character reaches 0 HP and fails their death saving throws, or is killed by an effect that causes instant death.
Before running this procedure: Confirm whether the death was appropriately telegraphed. Per campaign parameters, any encounter with a meaningful death risk must have given the party a clear opportunity to avoid or retreat. If the death was a surprise with no prior warning, treat it as a DM error and discuss with the group before applying permanent consequences.
Step 1 — Check Death Insurance
Ask the player: Is your character’s death insurance active?
Death insurance is a retainer service purchased from the Wizard Shop. Coverage is only valid if:

The character enrolled in the service
Payments are current (have not lapsed)

If coverage is active: Proceed to Step 2 (Insurance Payout).
If coverage is inactive or lapsed: Proceed to Step 3 (Standard Resurrection Options).
Step 2 — Insurance Payout
The insurance activates automatically. The character is recovered by guild agents and subjected to whatever revival method the Wizard Shop retainer covers (details to be established when the service is first purchased).
The revival is not guaranteed to be clean — proceed to Step 4 (Resurrection Consequences) regardless of the method used.
Step 3 — Standard Resurrection Options
Without insurance, resurrection requires the party to pursue it actively. Options available through the guild:

























MethodAvailabilityNotesWizard Shop retainer (post-death)Available, but costlyFull price without prior insurance; DM sets costExternal resurrection servicesRequires travel and goldClerics, temples, powerful NPCsParty resourcesIf a party member has accessRevivify window is 1 minute — likely expired
The party may choose not to pursue resurrection. A dead character whose player wants to continue can roll a new character, introduced at the DM’s discretion.
Step 4 — Resurrection Consequences
Every resurrection — regardless of method — carries meaningful consequences. The DM determines the specific form based on narrative context, choosing one or more of:
Roleplay consequences (examples):

A vision, haunting memory, or changed outlook from the near-death experience
An obligation to the entity or service that facilitated the revival
Shifted relationships with other characters or factions
A period of physical or mental recovery with narrative effects

Failure chance:

There is a small chance any resurrection simply does not work. The DM sets this probability (suggested: 10–15%) and rolls privately.
If the resurrection fails, inform the player privately and run the failure moment in-session at the most dramatically appropriate time.



                  
                  Failure Handling 
                  
                

If resurrection fails, treat the character as permanently dead. Work with the player to introduce a new character. Do not re-roll — a failed resurrection is final.


Step 5 — Update Campaign Records
After the session:

Update the player character note in Player Characters/ to reflect death or recovery status
If the character died permanently, note the circumstances in the campaign index under Known Factions/Lore
If consequences were assigned, note them in the character note for future DMs to reference



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Death should feel meaningful without feeling punitive. The goal is that players care about survival without dreading the table. Lean on roleplay consequences over mechanical ones — a character haunted by what they saw is more interesting than a character with -1 to all rolls for three sessions.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Bilgo Bangwiz Bazaar
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Bilgo Bangwiz Bazaar


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

A hand-painted sign over the door reads “Bilgo Bangwiz Bazaar (Death Not Guaranteed).” Inside, books are stacked on books stacked on shelves — some clearly load-bearing. Wands, scrolls, unlabelled potions, and things that may once have been alive crowd every surface. A kobold in scorched purple robes is reading aloud from a smoking book titled Advanced Pyrotheurgy for Amateurs, grinning with far too many teeth, while a terrified-looking customer is dragged out the door by a much calmer lizardfolk colleague.


Overview
The headquarters’ wizard shop — arcane supplies, spell scrolls, magical items, curse removal, and the guild’s death insurance program. Part of the Shopping District, within easy reach of the castle’s main courtyard.
Proprietor: Bilgo Bangwiz
A kobold — that much everyone agrees on. His exact age, origin, and how he learned so much magic are all unknown, including to Bilgo himself. He has survived for far longer than most kobolds should and seems to have genuinely forgotten that death is supposed to be permanent. This explains a great deal.

“I’ve exploded loads of times. Statistically speaking, you’re probably fine.”

Personality: Constant motion, constant talk, constant experimentation — the energy of a wizard who drank too much coffee decades ago and never came down. Refuses to throw anything away (“What if I need it later?”), frequently loses items while holding them, has invented multiple organisational systems and understands none of them. Customers regularly leave more confused than they arrived, or having accidentally bought something they didn’t intend to. Bilgo considers both outcomes a success.
Death Insurance
The cornerstone of Bilgo’s business and the source of the shop’s slogan. This is the guild’s confirmed retainer-based death insurance service referenced in Player Death (Step 1 — Check Death Insurance).
For a fee, Bilgo collects a lock of hair and archives it. If the insured individual dies, Bilgo uses restorative magic and experimental arcane procedures to bring them back — usually.
Package:

Initial Enrollment — 500 gp
Annual Renewal — 100 gp (coverage lapses if unpaid, per Player Death)

Benefits: Resurrection services, magical recovery assistance, priority restoration, complimentary tea during revival.
Disclaimer: Returned customers may experience slight personality changes, new food preferences, temporary memory gaps, unusual dreams, or mild existential confusion. Bilgo insists these are “mostly cosmetic.” (These line up neatly with the Resurrection Consequences described in Player Death Step 4 — use them as the specific roleplay flavor when a PC comes back through Bilgo’s insurance.)
Stock & Other Services
Spell Scrolls (inventory changes daily): Level 1 (50 gp) through Level 9 (25,000 gp), doubling/escalating roughly by level. Availability not guaranteed.
Arcane Components: Common/rare spell components, monster parts, ritual supplies, arcane foci, component pouches, magical ink, enchanted paper — priced by rarity and whether Bilgo can actually locate them.
Magical Items: Common, uncommon, curious enchanted trinkets, experimental prototypes, questionable inventions. No refunds unless legally required.
Remove Curse: Basic Curse Removal (250 gp), Powerful Curse Removal (1,000 gp+), Ancient or Legendary Curses (consultation required). This is a straightforward paid service — once the party covers the listed cost for the diagnosed severity tier, the curse is lifted on the spot. See Curse and Disease Removal for the full procedure, including the optional exception for Ancient/Legendary cases.
Arcane Identification: Item Identification (50 gp), Complex Artifact Analysis (250 gp)
Magical Consultation: Arcane Advice (25 gp), Research Assistance (50 gp/hour)
Custom Commissions: Custom spell scrolls, magical research, enchanted items, arcane experimentation, curse removal, theoretical magical projects. Success rate varies; Bilgo won’t give exact percentages.


                  
                  Customer Notice (in-world) 
                  
                

By entering the shop, customers acknowledge: unexpected magical effects may occur, spatial anomalies are possible, temporal anomalies are unlikely but not impossible, death is not guaranteed, and safety is also not guaranteed.
“If everything goes according to plan, I’ve probably made a mistake somewhere.”


Guild Rumours

“Bilgo once misplaced a cursed sword for twenty years.” / “The cursed sword was apparently looking for him.”
“Nobody knows how many books are actually inside the shop.”
“Several adventurers have died and come back through Bilgo’s insurance program.” / “One of them came back speaking fluent Giant despite never having learned it.” / “Bilgo says that’s within acceptable parameters.”
“The building violates at least seventeen known safety regulations.” / “Only seventeen?”

Guild Reputation
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — “The most dangerous place in Headquarters. Also one of the most useful.”
Hidden Details
(Add discoveries here as the party explores or interacts with Bilgo further.)
Connected Locations

The Guild Headquarters



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Bilgo’s “I’ve exploded loads of times” attitude makes him a great source of comic-relief danger that’s never actually a surprise to the table — he can hand the party an item with an honestly-disclosed-but-absurd risk, which satisfies the campaign’s “telegraph danger” rule while staying lighthearted. His hoarding habit (“what if I need it later?”) is a built-in excuse for any plot-relevant magic item to plausibly already be somewhere in his shop, buried.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Bottom of the Barrel
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Bottom of the Barrel


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

Warm lanterns hang from the beams over oversized tables built for sharing stories and exaggerating accomplishments. The walls are a museum of pirate memorabilia, retired gear, maps, monster trophies, and tankards signed by famous adventurers. A stone fireplace dominates one wall, and the smell of breakfast fills the room — because there’s only one thing on the menu, at every hour of every day. Near the door, a woman with a faded skull-and-crossbones tattoo refills mugs and somehow already knows your name.


Overview
The headquarters’ tavern, inn, breakfast establishment, and informal quest hub. Part of the Shopping District, within easy reach of the castle’s main courtyard. Functionally the campaign’s social home base — this is where downtime roleplay, guild gossip, and the Quest Board (see below) live.
Proprietor: Captain Briney “Bones” Blackwake
A former pirate captain who spent decades sailing the seas of Faerûn through treasure hunting, sea monsters, mutiny attempts, and poor financial decisions — and then, to everyone’s surprise, retired into running a tavern extremely well.

“Life’s easier after a hot meal. If it ain’t easier after that, have another hot meal.”

Personality: Friendly, approachable, and carries the effortless authority of someone who’s survived more disasters than most people can imagine. Knows the names and stories of almost every regular, gives unexpectedly wise advice, and always seems to know when a quest has gone badly or when someone needs encouragement — though she’d rather nobody made a fuss about it. Quietly covers the tab for struggling adventurers and refuses to admit she’s sentimental.
The tattoo: Bones has an ordinary skull-and-crossbones tattoo on her upper arm. Whenever a fight breaks out in the tavern, she simply rolls up her sleeve and shows it — and the fight stops, fast. Nobody is sure why. Nobody wants to test the theory.
The Breakfast Policy
Bones believes breakfast is the best meal of the day, and pirates rarely get a proper one — an injustice she now corrects unilaterally. Breakfast is the only thing on the menu, served all day, every day, no exceptions. Ask for lunch, dinner, or dessert and you get breakfast, sweet breakfast, or more breakfast respectively. She sees no issue with this.
Menu
All-Day Breakfast: Sailor’s Breakfast (5 sp), Guild Breakfast (8 sp), Captain’s Breakfast Feast (2 gp), Stack of Pancakes (4 sp), Honey Pancakes (6 sp), Cinnamon Pancakes (6 sp), Breakfast Sandwich (5 sp), Eggs Any Style (3 sp), Hash Browns (2 sp), Sausage Platter (4 sp), Bacon Platter (4 sp), Oatmeal & Fruit (3 sp)
Sweet Breakfast: Berry Waffles (5 sp), Apple Crumble Pancakes (7 sp), Honey Toast (3 sp), Sweet Cream Pastries (5 sp)
Drinks: Ale (4 cp), Fine Ale (2 sp), Mead (2 sp), Coffee (3 cp), Tea (2 cp), Fruit Juice (1 sp)
Signature Drink — The Scurvy Slayer (5 sp): A gigantic tankard of orange, lemon, lime, grapefruit, and “more citrus.” “If this doesn’t cure your scurvy, you’re probably already dead.”
Celebration Package (5 gp): For parties returning from a successful contract — reserved table, complimentary breakfast platter, and the adventure gets added to the guild’s Story Wall.
Adventurer Story Wall: Members can submit their own adventure stories for the wall. Accuracy is highly variable; entertainment value is not.
The Quest Board
Mounted outside the tavern entrance, this is where most public contracts are posted first. Postings may include monster hunts, escort contracts, missing persons, ruin exploration, bounty notices, investigation requests, guild requests, and odd jobs. More sensitive or higher-stakes missions bypass the board and go directly to a party instead.


                  
                  DM Note — Use this as the contract hook 
                  
                

The campaign’s Always Include: Guild contract framing rule says every session opens with a contract. The Quest Board is the natural in-fiction delivery mechanism for public/lower-stakes jobs — describe the board, let the party pick a posting, and you have your session hook with zero extra setup. Save direct-delivery contracts (an officer pulling the party aside) for jobs that need to feel personal, urgent, or secretive.


Guild Rumours

“Captain Bones once negotiated peace between two rival adventuring parties over pancakes.”
“Nobody knows what the tattoo actually does.” / “It probably doesn’t do anything.” / “Then why does nobody start fights?” / “Fair point.”
“The breakfast portions get larger when Bones thinks you’ve had a rough week.”
“She’s adopted at least half the guild.”

Guild Reputation
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — “The closest thing the Headquarters has to home.”
Hidden Details
(Add discoveries here as the party explores or interacts with Bones further.)
Connected Locations

The Guild Headquarters



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Bones is the campaign’s emotional anchor NPC — a good default voice for delivering roleplay-based consequences gently (per Player Death) or for noticing when a player’s character needs a quiet character moment. The tattoo gag is a great low-stakes way to defuse an in-fiction tavern brawl without it ever threatening to become a real combat encounter.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Missy's Magnificent Miscellaneous Merchandise
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Missy’s Magnificent Miscellaneous Merchandise


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

A hand-painted sign creaks above the door: “Good gear. Good sense. Safe travels!” Inside, every shelf is crammed with rope, lanterns, bedrolls, and a hundred small useful things, and the whole shop smells faintly of leather and candle wax. A sleepy white cat watches from a basket near the ceiling. Behind the counter, an orange tabby — standing upright, sleeves rolled to the elbow — is doing something complicated with a ball of blue yarn and not looking up yet.


Overview
The headquarters’ general store — everyday adventuring supplies sold by a uniquely transformed proprietor. Part of the Shopping District, within easy reach of the castle’s main courtyard.
Proprietor: Missy Whiskerpaws
An orange tabby cat who, years ago, accidentally drank an experimental transformation potion. She now stands roughly 4 feet tall, can walk upright or on all fours depending on her mood, has opposable thumbs, and speaks Common fluently — but remains unmistakably feline in appearance.
Personality: Treats every customer like a grandchild whether they want it or not — slips extra biscuits into packs, fusses over warm clothing, insists everyone take a spare length of rope (“you never know”). Despite the warmth, she’s wonderfully chaotic: naps on the front counter mid-business-hours, chases mice through important transactions, knocks merchandise off shelves while maintaining unbroken eye contact, and will flatly refuse to sell to adventurers she judges to be making “poor life choices.” Regulars suspect she knows far more about her customers than she lets on — nobody knows how.
Stock
Everyday adventuring supplies — Missy calls it “everything sensible”:

Backpacks and travel packs
Rope, twine, and climbing gear
Bedrolls and tents
Lanterns, oil, and candles
Waterskins and mess kits
Rations and trail food
Maps and journals
Basic tools and repair kits
Fishing supplies
Soap, sewing kits, and travel necessities

She refuses to stock magic items, weapons, armour, or anything likely to cause “unnecessary explosions.”
Guild Rumours

“Missy once sent a party back to buy extra rope. Three days later they survived a cave collapse because of it.”
“Nobody knows how she always knows exactly what you’ll need.”

Guild Reputation
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — “Best place in Headquarters to forget what you came in for and leave with exactly what you needed.”
Hidden Details
(Add discoveries here as the party explores or interacts with Missy further.)
Connected Locations

The Guild Headquarters



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Missy’s uncanny knack for knowing what a party will need makes her a natural source of subtle foreshadowing — have her press a specific item on the party (extra rope, a lantern, a particular tool) right before a session where that exact item becomes relevant, without ever breaking the fiction. This supports the campaign’s rule that deadly encounters must always be telegraphed in advance.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Silvers Blades
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Silvers Blades


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The contrast with the forge across the hall is immediate — cool, quiet, and almost unnervingly clean. Blades hang in perfect symmetry like museum pieces. At the centre of the room, a basin of moonlit water glows soft silver-blue, its steam drifting blue-tinted through the air. A tall, impeccably dressed man glances up from a half-finished blade, takes in your stance and the state of your gear in one practiced look, and says nothing yet — but you can tell he’s already found something to comment on.


Overview
The headquarters’ weaponsmith, bladesmith, and custom arms dealer. Part of the Shopping District, within easy reach of the castle’s main courtyard — directly across the hall from Steele’s Armory.
Proprietor: Silver
A Water Genasi, tall and slender, impeccably dressed in elegant robes and tailored coats with silver embroidery, flowing water-like hair, and a permanent expression of mild disappointment. First-time visitors often mistake him for a noble, scholar, or wealthy merchant rather than a smith — but he’s widely regarded as one of the finest weaponsmiths in Faerûn.

“A weapon is merely a conversation. Whether it becomes a discussion or an argument depends entirely upon the wielder.”

His forge centres on a basin of enchanted moonlit water; he shapes and refines metal using magically generated steam with extraordinary precision, rather than Steele’s open flame.
Personality: Polite, elegant, professionally precise — and incapable of ignoring a flaw. A crooked grip, poor posture, a poorly maintained weapon, a smudge on a display case — Silver notices everything and will comment on it, usually with perfectly delivered dry sarcasm. He corrects customers’ grips unasked, judges adventurers by how well they maintain their gear, and has memorised the exact location of every item in the shop. Beneath the sarcasm he genuinely cares about the quality of his work and his customers — though he’d never admit the second part aloud.
Notable quirk: Silver insists he has no interest whatsoever in Steele. He also somehow always knows exactly where Steele is. A coincidence, surely.
Stock & Services
Simple Weapons: Club (1 sp), Dagger (2 gp), Greatclub (2 sp), Handaxe (5 gp), Javelin (5 sp), Light Hammer (2 gp), Mace (5 gp), Quarterstaff (2 sp), Sickle (1 gp), Spear (1 gp)
Martial Melee Weapons: Battleaxe (10 gp), Flail (10 gp), Glaive (20 gp), Greataxe (30 gp), Greatsword (50 gp), Halberd (20 gp), Lance (10 gp), Longsword (15 gp), Maul (10 gp), Morningstar (15 gp), Pike (5 gp), Rapier (25 gp), Scimitar (25 gp), Shortsword (10 gp), Trident (5 gp), War Pick (5 gp), Warhammer (15 gp), Whip (2 gp)
Ranged Weapons: Shortbow (25 gp), Longbow (50 gp), Light Crossbow (25 gp), Heavy Crossbow (50 gp), Hand Crossbow (75 gp)
Masterwork Upgrades: Decorative Engravings (50 gp+), Family Heraldry (75 gp+), Custom Grip Work (25 gp+), Enhanced Balance (100 gp+), Ceremonial Finishes (100 gp+), Collector Grade Craftsmanship (quote required)
Repair Services: Minor Weapon Repair (10 gp), Major Weapon Repair (50 gp), Blade Reforging (75 gp), Restoration of Damaged Heirlooms (quote required)
Custom Commissions: Custom swords, duelling weapons, ceremonial weapons, family heirlooms, exotic weapon designs, adventuring gear upgrades, decorative collector pieces
Moonforge Options (by request): Silver filigree, decorative water motifs, noble house heraldry, precision balancing, mirror-polished finishes, matching weapon sets

“Function first. Beauty immediately afterwards.”

Guild Rumours

“Silver once spent six hours polishing a sword that was already polished.”
“The enchanted water in his forge glows brighter when Steele walks past.”
“He complains about Steele constantly.”
“He also has lunch with Steele almost every day.” / “Professional lunch.”
“Nobody has ever convinced either of them they’re obviously in love.”
“The betting pool has been running for seven years.”

Guild Reputation
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — “If Silver forged it, you’ll probably die before the blade does.”
Hidden Details
(Add discoveries here as the party explores or interacts with Silver further.)
Connected Locations

The Guild Headquarters
Steele’s Armory — directly across the hall; see the long-running guild betting pool on whether Steele and Silver will ever admit their feelings



                  
                  DM Note 
                  
                

Silver’s unsolicited but always-correct critiques (bad grip, poorly maintained gear, wrong weapon for the job) work the same way as Steele’s — a blunt, in-fiction way to telegraph mechanical danger before a fight, consistent with the campaign’s “no surprise lethality” rule. The Steele/Silver slow-burn is a standing background bit the party can poke at for comic relief during downtime; it doesn’t need to resolve quickly, and probably shouldn’t.

Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.title: Steele's Armory
Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
Steele’s Armory


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

Heat rolls off the forge before you’re even through the door. An ancient furnace burns at the heart of the workshop, its molten light spilling through vents and washing rows of armour stands in orange. Hammer rings against steel in a steady rhythm. The smith doesn’t look up — broad-shouldered, soot-streaked, eyes smouldering faintly like banked embers — until the metal in his tongs is ready.


Overview
The headquarters’ armoury, shieldworks, and master smithing shop. Part of the Shopping District, within easy reach of the castle’s main courtyard — directly across the hall from Silvers Blades.
Proprietor: Steele
A Fire Genasi, well over six feet tall, broad-shouldered, soot-stained, with smouldering ember-like eyes — looks as though carved from volcanic rock and given life by a stubborn fire elemental. Permanently warm to the touch, heavily muscled, covered in scars from a lifetime at the forge. Appears to be in his thirties but carries himself like someone who has worked every day of his life.

“Armour won’t save your life. Wearing it properly might.”

The forge itself is powered by the captured heart of a Fire Elemental.
Personality: A man of almost no words — a grunt, a nod, maybe one sentence if you’re lucky. Despite the silence, his judgement on armour is trusted absolutely: if he says a breastplate won’t fit, it won’t; if he says a shield is unbalanced, it is; if he says you’re not strong enough for a suit of armour, you probably aren’t. He asks every customer to lift something heavy before they leave, critiques posture unprompted, can spot armour weaknesses at a glance, and remembers every piece he’s ever crafted. He almost never smiles.
Notable quirk: Steele is frequently seen glancing across the hall toward Silvers Blades. He denies it every time. Nobody believes him.
Stock & Services
Light Armour: Padded (5 gp), Leather (10 gp), Studded Leather (45 gp)
Medium Armour: Hide (10 gp), Chain Shirt (50 gp), Scale Mail (50 gp), Breastplate (400 gp), Half Plate (750 gp)
Heavy Armour: Ring Mail (30 gp), Chain Mail (75 gp), Splint (200 gp), Plate (1,500 gp)
Shields: Shield (10 gp), Reinforced Shield (50 gp), Decorative Shield (100 gp), Custom Heraldic Shield (150 gp+)
Mount Equipment: Saddles, barding, harnesses, travel tack, custom mount armour — priced by creature size and materials.
Repair Services: Minor Armour Repair (10 gp), Major Armour Repair (50 gp), Shield Repair (15 gp), Battle Damage Restoration (quote required)

“Steele once repaired a suit of plate armour after a dragon sat on it.”
“He can tell your profession by how you stand.”
“The forge gets hotter when he’s angry.”

Steele’s blunt, unimpeachable expertise makes him a good source of mechanical foreshadowing — if he warns a PC that a piece of gear is wrong for them or a fight ahead, take it as gospel, and consider having him do so right before a session where it matters. Games/D-and-D/D-and-D-Campaigns/D-and-D-.content:
The Bubbling Cauldron


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The shop is half apothecary, half greenhouse — living vines crawl the walls, mushrooms grow from enchanted logs, and flowers along the windowsill seem to turn as you pass. A mortar and pestle sit half-used on a cluttered workbench. An ageless elf with long silver hair looks up from a sprig of glowing leaves, smiles, and says nothing — but somewhere nearby, a fern rustles, as if it just told them something about you.


Overview
The headquarters’ potion shop, apothecary, and herbalist. Part of the Shopping District, within easy reach of the castle’s main courtyard. Provides the guild’s confirmed disease-removal service referenced in the Guild Headquarters services table.
Proprietor: Aster
An ageless elf with no concept of gender, who identifies simply as a caretaker of life, growth, and healing. Has spent centuries studying botany, medicine, alchemy, and disease, and is one of the most knowledgeable healers affiliated with the Faerûn Adventure League.

“Every ailment tells a story. Fortunately, I speak fluent root, leaf, petal, and fungus.”

Aster’s gift: Every plant in the shop constantly whispers information only Aster can hear — who’s sick, stressed, injured, exhausted, or attempting to steal. Aster carries on full conversations with hanging ferns and occasionally pauses mid-sale to consult a flower’s opinion. The plants are usually correct, and nobody has ever successfully stolen from the shop. Aster can often identify illnesses before symptoms become obvious, never forgets a face, and customarily serves tea before discussing business.
Guild Rumours

“Aster once diagnosed a disease simply by listening to a daisy.”
“The roses near the entrance gossip about customers.”

“The hanging ivy by the doorway has a better memory than most guild scribes.”

The Guild Headquarters


                  
                  Read Aloud 
                  
                

The headquarters rises above the surrounding land like a small city unto itself — towers, courtyards, covered walkways, and the constant low hum of people who live and work and train here. The gate crest bears the guild’s emblem. Inside, you know where everything is. It smells like stone and coal smoke and something faintly magical. It smells like home.


Overview
The guild headquarters — home of the Faerûn Adventure League — is a large self-sufficient castle complex that serves as the party’s permanent home base. It sits in the outskirts of Waterdeep, on the Sword Coast: close enough to the city for contracts and supply runs, far enough to have its own grounds and identity distinct from Waterdeep proper.
It functions as a full institution — member quarters, training halls, administrative offices, and a complete range of services. Arriving here between sessions means the party can resupply, seek information, recover, and interact with the broader guild community.
The castle’s internal layout, named rooms, and resident personalities are to be discovered and documented during play. Add new notes and wikilinks to this file as the party explores.

Ethereal Dreadknight

  Armor Class 18
  Hit Points 136 (16d8 + 64)
  Speed 30 ft., fly 30 ft. (hover)
  
  
    
      
        STR

  Saving Throws Str +9, Con +8, Wis +7, Cha +8
  Skills Perception +7, Intimidation +8, Athletics +9
  Damage Resistances acid, fire, lightning, thunder; bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing from nonmagical attacks
  Damage Immunities necrotic, poison

  Ethereal Jaunt. As a bonus action, the dreadknight can magically shift from the Material Plane to the Ethereal Plane, or vice versa. While on the Ethereal Plane, the dreadknight can see and hear into the Material Plane to a range of 60 feet, but everything looks gray and ephemeral.
  Incorporeal Movement. The dreadknight can move through other creatures and objects as if they were difficult terrain. It takes 5 (1d10) force damage if it ends its turn inside an object.
  Undead Fortitude. If damage reduces the dreadknight to 0 hit points, it must make a Constitution saving throw with a DC of 5 + the damage taken, unless the damage is radiant or from a critical hit. On a success, the dreadknight drops to 1 hit point instead.
  Spectral Armor. The dreadknight's AC includes its Charisma modifier while it is not wearing armor or wielding a shield.

  Phase Strike. Ranged Spell Attack: +8 to hit, range 120 ft., one target. Hit: 18 (4d6 + 4) force damage. The dreadknight can make this attack from the Ethereal Plane against targets on the Material Plane.
  Soul Drain (Recharge 5-6). The dreadknight targets one creature it can see within 30 feet of it. The target must succeed on a DC 16 Constitution saving throw or take 36 (8d8) necrotic damage and have its hit point maximum reduced by an amount equal to the damage taken. The dreadknight regains hit points equal to half the damage dealt. This reduction lasts until the target finishes a long rest. The target dies if this effect reduces its hit point maximum to 0.
  Legendary Actions
  Detect. The dreadknight makes a Wisdom (Perception) check.
  Phase Strike. The dreadknight uses Phase Strike.
  Ethereal Step (Costs 2 Actions). The dreadknight uses Ethereal Jaunt and moves up to its speed.
  Soul Rend (Costs 3 Actions). The dreadknight makes one Phantom Greatsword attack against each creature within 10 feet of it.
  Reactions
  Phase Dodge. When a creature the dreadknight can see targets it with an attack, the dreadknight can shift partially into the Ethereal Plane, imposing disadvantage on the attack roll. If the attack misses, the dreadknight can immediately move up to half its speed without provoking opportunity attacks.

Ethereal Dreadknight
Lore
Ethereal Dreadknights are the cursed remnants of once-noble warriors who bargained with dark powers to escape death. Their pact granted them immortality, but at a terrible cost—they exist partially in the Ethereal Plane, forever trapped between life and death, solid and spectral.
These terrifying undead warriors serve dark masters or pursue their own inscrutable vendettas, phasing in and out of reality to strike at their enemies. Their touch drains the very life force from the living, and their presence radiates an aura of death that withers all nearby.
Tactics
An Ethereal Dreadknight is a cunning combatant that uses its planar mobility to devastating effect:

Opening Move: Uses Dreadful Presence and Death’s Aura to soften up groups of enemies
Hit and Run: Shifts to the Ethereal Plane with Ethereal Jaunt, repositions, then returns to make devastating melee attacks
Ranged Harassment: Uses Phase Strike from the Ethereal Plane where it’s safe from most attacks
Finishing Blow: Uses Soul Drain on wounded enemies to heal itself and eliminate threats
Legendary Actions: Maintains pressure with Phase Strikes and repositioning, saving Soul Rend for clustered enemies

Encounter Ideas

The Phantom Castle: The dreadknight haunts an abandoned fortress, phasing through walls to ambush intruders
Vengeful Spirit: Hired by a necromancer to eliminate those who wronged it in life
Bridge Guardian: Guards a planar rift between the Material and Ethereal Planes
The Hunt: Pursues the party relentlessly, appearing when they least expect it

Goblin Warlord
  Small humanoid (goblinoid), neutral evil
  
  Armor Class 15 (studded leather)
  Hit Points 91 (14d6 + 42)
  Speed 30 ft.
  
  
    
      
        STR
        DEX
        CON
        INT
        WIS
        CHA
      
      
        10 (+0)
        16 (+3)
        16 (+3)
