        14 (+2)
      
    
  
  
  Saving Throws Dex +6, Int +7, Wis +4
  Skills Intimidation +5, Perception +4, Stealth +6
  Damage Resistances psychic
  Senses darkvision 60 ft., passive Perception 14
  Languages Common, Goblin, Deep Speech
  Challenge 5
  
  Nimble Escape. The warlord can take the Disengage or Hide action as a bonus action on each of its turns.
  Psychic Bulwark. The warlord has advantage on saving throws against being Charmed or Frightened.
  Warlord's Presence. Goblinoid allies within 30 ft. of the warlord that can see or hear it gain a +2 bonus to attack rolls and saving throws.
  Actions
  Multiattack. The warlord makes two Psionic Blade attacks, or one Psionic Blade attack and one Psychic Lash.
  Psionic Blade. Melee Weapon Attack: +6 to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 7 (1d6 + 3) slashing damage plus 10 (3d6) psychic damage.
  Psychic Lash. Ranged Spell Attack: +7 to hit, range 60 ft., one target. Hit: 18 (4d6 + 4) psychic damage, and the target must succeed on a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw or be Frightened of the warlord until the end of its next turn.
  Mind Shatter (Recharge 5-6). The warlord targets one creature it can see within 60 ft. The target must make a DC 15 Intelligence saving throw. On a failed save, the target takes 35 (10d6) psychic damage and is Stunned until the end of its next turn. On a successful save, the target takes half damage and is not Stunned.
  Reactions
  Psionic Shield. When the warlord would take damage, it reduces that damage by 11 (2d10). If this reduces the damage to 0, the attacker takes 5 (1d10) psychic damage.

Lore
Goblin warlords gifted with psionic power are rare aberrations in goblinoid society — feared even by their own kind. These individuals developed their psychic abilities through exposure to aberrant energies: proximity to a mind flayer colony, a Far Realm rift seeping into their warren, or extended contact with a stolen illithid artifact. Where ordinary goblin chieftains rule through cunning and brute fear, a Goblin Warlord holds its tribe in an iron psychic grip, implanting suggestions directly into followers’ minds and punishing treachery with crippling mental agony.
Within the tribe, the warlord is regarded as touched by dark gods — something beyond mortal comprehension. Followers obey not merely out of habit but because dissent carries a physical cost. As a result, a tribe under a Goblin Warlord’s control is unnervingly disciplined compared to the rabbles other adventurers expect. The warlord also speaks Deep Speech, a tongue it likely learned from the aberrant sources of its power, and it uses this knowledge to negotiate — or make threats — in circles far above the typical goblin’s station.
Goblin Warlords are deeply ambitious. They seek out further sources of aberrant power to grow their psionic gifts, and many dream of uniting disparate goblin tribes under one psychically enforced banner. A few have come dangerously close to succeeding. They are calculating enemies who never spend a minion’s life wastefully — every goblin is a chess piece, and the warlord is always three moves ahead.
Tactics
The warlord avoids direct melee and opens combat from range, using Psychic Lash to Frighten the most dangerous-looking opponent before it can close the distance. Warlord’s Presence passively buffs all goblin allies on the field — the warlord maintains line of sight to as many minions as possible, so positioning matters. Mind Shatter is saved for the character who looks most capable of reaching the warlord (the heavily armoured warrior, the aggressive paladin), deployed the moment it recharges.
When threatened in melee, the warlord uses Psionic Shield to blunt incoming blows, then uses its Nimble Escape bonus action to Hide and slip back to a ranged position. Psychic Command is used liberally to direct minions into flanking positions, or to trigger a free attack from a minion already engaged with a distracted player. If reduced below half HP, the warlord psychically commands its fastest goblin to make a suicidal charge into the most dangerous enemy as a distraction, then attempts to flee — it knows no war is won from a corpse.
Encounter Ideas
The Mind-Locked Tribe: The party enters a goblin warren and finds something unsettling — the goblins are silent, coordinated, their eyes occasionally going blank mid-sentence. The whole tribe is under the warlord’s psychic grip. A few goblins are dimly aware that something is wrong but are too controlled to act. If the players can reach and defeat the warlord, the tribe’s conditioning may collapse — leaving a confused, traumatised rabble who were victims as much as enemies.
Siege at Stillwater Bridge: A goblin force has blockaded the only river crossing for miles, led by the warlord directing from a fortified hilltop. It uses Mind Shatter to disable whoever tries to lead the assault, and Psychic Command keeps goblin archers in a devastating coordinated volley. The party must find a way to reach the warlord through the chaotic press below — perhaps flanking through the river, or using the terrain to break line of sight and deny its Warlord’s Presence buff.
The Warlord’s Offer: The Goblin Warlord approaches the party under a flag of truce with a grudging proposal: something more powerful has moved into the region — a mind flayer outpost, an undead warlord — and is interfering with its own ambitions. It wants a temporary alliance. The warlord is utterly untrustworthy and the players know it. But the common enemy is real. What do they do with a villain who genuinely wants to help them this once?

  Challenge 1/4
  
  Nimble Escape. The goblin can take the Disengage or Hide action as a bonus action on each of its turns.
  Actions
  Scimitar. Melee Weapon Attack: +4 to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 5 (1d6 + 2) slashing damage.
  Shortbow. Ranged Weapon Attack: +4 to hit, range 80/320 ft., one target. Hit: 5 (1d6 + 2) piercing damage.

Lore
Goblins are small, black-hearted humanoids that lair in caves, abandoned mines, despoiled dungeons, and other dismal settings. Individually weak, goblins gather in large numbers to torment other creatures. They are motivated by greed and malice, and are renowned for their cowardice in the face of superior forces.
Goblins belong to a family of creatures called goblinoids, which includes their larger cousins the hobgoblins and bugbears. They have flat faces, broad noses, pointed ears, and small, sharp fangs. Their foreheads slope back, and their eyes are usually dull and glazed. They always walk upright, but their arms hang down almost to their knees. Their skin color ranges from yellow through orange to deep red, and they are typically filthy.
Goblins live in dark, dank places where they can ambush prey and scavenge for food. They worship deities of trickery and destruction, building crude shrines in their lairs. Goblin tribes are led by the strongest among them, though leadership often changes through acts of treachery and assassination.
Tactics
Goblins are cowardly and cunning, preferring to attack from ambush or with overwhelming numbers. They make extensive use of their Nimble Escape feature, allowing them to dart in and out of combat without provoking opportunity attacks. A typical goblin will fire its shortbow from range, using cover whenever possible, and only engage in melee when cornered or when they have a significant numerical advantage.
When fighting in groups, goblins coordinate to focus fire on isolated or wounded targets. They’re quick to flee when the battle turns against them, often leaving slower members of their tribe behind as distractions. Goblins set simple traps around their lairs—pit traps, tripwires connected to bells, or precariously balanced objects—to give them warning and slow down intruders.
Smart goblin leaders position ranged attackers on elevated terrain or behind barricades while melee goblins harass from the flanks. If forced to retreat, they’ll collapse tunnels, bar doors, or release captured animals to cover their escape.
Encounter Ideas
Ambush at the Crossroads: A band of 6-8 goblins has been waylaying travelers at a forest crossroads. They’ve built crude barricades from fallen logs and positioned archers in trees. The goblins demand “shiny things” as toll, but their leader carries a stolen signet ring that belongs to a local noble—recovering it could earn the party a reward and gratitude.
The Stolen Supplies: Goblins have been raiding a remote farmstead nightly, stealing chickens, tools, and food. The party is hired to track them back to their cave lair. Inside, they discover the goblins are stockpiling supplies for a larger force of bugbears who plan to raid the nearby village. The party must decide whether to eliminate the threat quietly or warn the village.
Goblin Diplomacy: A goblin scout approaches the party with a white flag (actually a dirty rag), claiming his tribe wants to make a deal. Their warren has been invaded by giant spiders, and they’ll pay the party in “shinies and secrets” to clear them out. The goblins can provide information about other dungeon areas, but can they be trusted to honor their bargain?

  Amorphous. Zylox can move through a space as narrow as 1 inch wide without squeezing. They can squeeze through spaces as narrow as a quarter of an inch.
  Shape Self. As an action, Zylox can reshape their body to give themselves a head, one or two arms, and one or two legs, or revert to a limbless blob. While Zylox has a humanoid shape, they can wear armor and wield weapons normally. As a bonus action, Zylox can extrude a pseudopod up to 6 inches wide and 10 feet long or reabsorb it into their body.
  Hold Breath. Zylox can hold their breath for 1 hour, making them ideal for wildspace operations.
  Cunning Action. On each of their turns in combat, Zylox can use a bonus action to take the Dash, Disengage, or Hide action.
  Sneak Attack (1/Turn). Zylox deals an extra 10 (3d6) damage when they hit a target with a weapon attack and have advantage on the attack roll, or when the target is within 5 feet of an ally of Zylox that isn't incapacitated and Zylox doesn't have disadvantage on the attack roll.
  Actions
  Multiattack. Zylox makes two attacks with their shortsword or hand crossbow.
  Shortsword. Melee Weapon Attack: +6 to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 7 (1d6 + 4) piercing damage.
  Hand Crossbow. Ranged Weapon Attack: +6 to hit, range 30/120 ft., one target. Hit: 7 (1d6 + 4) piercing damage.
  Pseudopod Grapple. Melee Weapon Attack: +6 to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. Hit: The target is grappled (escape DC 12). While grappling a target with a pseudopod, Zylox can still use their arms to attack with weapons.
  Reactions
  Uncanny Dodge. When an attacker that Zylox can see hits them with an attack, they can use their reaction to halve the attack's damage against them.

Lore
Zylox is a plasmoid rogue operating in the Astral Sea and wildspace beyond. Like all plasmoids, Zylox is a sentient ooze capable of assuming humanoid form or flowing like liquid through the smallest cracks. Their translucent, gelatinous body shimmers with an amber hue, and they often maintain a vaguely humanoid shape with surprisingly expressive features when dealing with other creatures. Born in the depths of wildspace aboard a giff merchant vessel, Zylox learned early that their unique physiology made them perfect for infiltration, espionage, and the art of thievery.
Plasmoids like Zylox are relatively rare but increasingly common in Spelljammer ports across wildspace. They have no true homeworld, existing primarily aboard spelljamming vessels and space stations. Zylox has spent decades perfecting the art of shapeshifting to impersonate various humanoid species, slipping past security, and acquiring valuable artifacts from across the cosmos. They’re particularly interested in magical items that can enhance their already formidable abilities.
Despite their roguish profession, Zylox follows a personal code: never harm innocents, and always honor contracts once made. They view theft as an art form and prefer cunning over violence. Zylox has become known in certain underworld circles of the Rock of Bral and other major ports as a reliable, if expensive, specialist for delicate acquisitions.
Tactics
Zylox excels at infiltration and surprise attacks. Before combat begins, they use Morphic Disguise to blend in with their surroundings or impersonate someone with legitimate access to their target area. Their Amorphous trait allows them to slip through ventilation shafts, under doors, or through ship hull breaches that would be impossible for others to navigate.
In combat, Zylox relies heavily on Cunning Action to maintain mobility, using Hit and Run tactics with their shortsword or hand crossbow. They position themselves to gain advantage for Sneak Attack, often hiding behind cover or attacking from unexpected angles. When facing multiple enemies, Zylox uses Uncanny Dodge to mitigate the most dangerous attacks while retreating to a better position.
The Pseudopod Grapple is one of Zylox’s signature moves—they can extend a tentacle-like appendage to grapple foes at range while still maintaining weapon attacks with their “arms.” This is particularly effective on spelljamming vessels where grappling an opponent near a railing could lead to them being pushed into wildspace. If cornered, Zylox transforms into a blob form and attempts to escape through small spaces, using their Hold Breath ability to survive in hostile environments.
Encounter Ideas
Vault Heist in Wildspace: The party is hired to transport a valuable artifact through wildspace when they discover their cargo has been replaced with a worthless fake. Investigation reveals Zylox infiltrated their ship by squeezing through a damaged porthole, replaced the artifact, and is now hiding somewhere aboard disguised as a crew member. The party must identify the impostor before reaching their destination, but Zylox is an expert at deflecting suspicion and creating alibis.
Rival Operative: The party and Zylox are both hired to acquire the same target—a set of spelljamming helm blueprints locked in an archmage’s sanctum on a drifting asteroid. Rather than direct confrontation, this becomes a race to see who can infiltrate first, with both groups potentially encountering each other at inopportune moments. Zylox might offer to team up temporarily, but their true loyalty is only to the contract. Can the party trust a shapeshifting thief?
Escape from the Brig: Zylox has been captured and imprisoned aboard a nautiloid (mind flayer ship) after a botched infiltration attempt. They send a psychic distress beacon through an illithid tadpole they swallowed (and later killed with their acid resistance). The party intercepts the signal and must decide whether to mount a rescue. If freed, Zylox offers valuable intelligence about the mind flayers’ plans and proves to be a useful ally—at least until they spot something valuable worth stealing.

Our Games 
                  
                

This section tracks the campaigns from our group’s D&D games. Log your sessions and keep track of the story as it unfolds!



About the Game
Publisher: Wizards of the Coast
Edition: 5th Edition (5e)
Scale: Roleplaying — typically 3–6 players plus a Dungeon Master
Session Length: Usually 2–4 hours
Core Mechanic: Roll a d20, add relevant modifiers, and meet or beat a Difficulty Class (DC) or the target’s Armour Class (AC)
Each character has six core ability scores — Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma — which feed into skills, saving throws, and attack rolls. This system is flexible enough to handle almost any situation while keeping the flow of play intuitive.

Current Campaigns

D&D Campaign 1 — Sunday Adventurers League, Level 3+, episodic contracts

Past Campaigns
None…

Useful Links

📖 Basic Rules (Free)
🧙 D&D Beyond (Character Builder & Compendium)
📚 Roll20 Compendium


Core Rules
These are based on D&D 5th Edition (2024 revision)
Ability Checks
When a character attempts something with a chance of failure, the DM calls for an ability check. Roll a d20 and add the relevant ability modifier (and proficiency bonus if applicable). Meet or beat the DC to succeed.

































DifficultyDCVery Easy5Easy10Medium15Hard20Very Hard25Nearly Impossible30
Combat
Initiative: At the start of combat, all combatants roll d20 + Dexterity modifier. Turns proceed from highest to lowest.
On Your Turn: Each combatant gets one Action, one Bonus Action (if available), and movement up to their speed.









































ActionDescriptionAttackMake one or more weapon or spell attacksCast a SpellCast a spell with a casting time of 1 actionDashDouble your movement speed this turnDisengageMove without provoking opportunity attacksDodgeAttackers have disadvantage; you have advantage on Dex savesHelpGive an ally advantage on their next check or attackHideMake a Stealth check to become hiddenReadyPrepare an action to trigger on a specific condition
Attack Rolls & Damage
Roll d20 + attack modifier vs target’s AC. On a hit, roll the weapon or spell’s damage dice and add the relevant modifier. A natural 20 is a critical hit — roll all damage dice twice.
Saving Throws
When subjected to harmful effects, roll d20 + the relevant saving throw modifier vs the effect’s DC. Success usually means reduced or avoided harm.
Advantage & Disadvantage
Roll two d20s and take the higher (advantage) or lower (disadvantage) result. These never stack — you either have advantage, disadvantage, or neither.
Conditions
Conditions alter a creature’s capabilities. Common ones include:





















































ConditionKey EffectBlindedAuto-fail sight checks; attacks against you have advantageCharmedCan’t attack the charmer; charmer has advantage on social checksFrightenedDisadvantage on checks/attacks while source is in sightGrappledSpeed becomes 0IncapacitatedCan’t take actions or reactionsParalyzedIncapacitated; auto-fail Str/Dex saves; hits within 5ft are critsPoisonedDisadvantage on attack rolls and ability checksProneDisadvantage on attacks; melee hits are crits, ranged have disadvRestrainedSpeed 0; disadvantage on attacks and Dex savesStunnedIncapacitated; auto-fail Str/Dex saves; attacks against have advUnconsciousParalyzed; auto-fail Str/Dex saves; falls prone
Death & Dying
When a character drops to 0 HP they fall unconscious and begin making death saving throws at the start of each turn — roll d20, 10+ is a success. Three successes = stabilised; three failures = dead. A natural 1 counts as two failures; a natural 20 restores 1 HP. Any damage while at 0 HP counts as a failure (massive damage may kill outright).
Resting

Short Rest (1 hour): Spend Hit Dice to recover HP; some class features recharge.
Long Rest (8 hours): Recover all HP, half your Hit Dice, and most expended spell slots and class features.
